ideas.title: Spare-Set Pool: hot-section outages with a guaranteed return-to-service date
ideas.one_liner: A neutral pool of pre-inspected, pre-fit hot-gas-path sets (rotor, nozzles, shrouds, combustion hardware) for the common F- and E-class frames. Owners with one to four units rent a set per outage and send their retired set into the pool, under a contract with a return-to-service date and liquidated damages.
ideas.customer: Owners of 1-4 large-frame units who cannot carry a spare set: G&T co-ops, municipal and joint-action agencies, small PE-backed IPPs, industrial cogens. Units outside OEM LTSA scope first.
ideas.payer_and_signer: VP Generation or plant manager signs; CFO co-signs because it replaces a $5-10M spare-capital purchase. Budget lines: major-outage O&M ($5-12M per hot-section event, my estimate from trade sources) and spares capital.
ideas.problem: Outage length is set 12-14 months earlier, by whether a certified spare is on site when the unit opens. Multi-unit fleets solve this privately (GE says many multi-F-class operators use a seed rotor; Dubai's DEWA rotor-swap method added up to 64 days of availability over eight uses per Siemens, with one overhaul done in 29 working days). A single-unit owner cannot tie up $10M in a spare, so it waits on shop turnaround, which castings scarcity is stretching.
ideas.solution: Build or buy sets for the 6-8 biggest frame families. Price like an aircraft-engine lease: rent while the owner's set is in the shop, plus usage-based maintenance reserves per equivalent operating hour that fund the repair, plus a guarantee fee. Finance the sets with infrastructure or equipment-finance capital. Returned sets go through partner repair shops and back into the pool.
ideas.why_now: New heavy-duty units are sold out to 2030-31 (GE Vernova backlog plus slot reservations 116 GW in Q2 2026), so there is no replacement capacity during an overrun. WoodMac calls single-crystal blade production the most stubborn constraint and GE Aerospace is paying $11.75B for casting maker CPP. PJM capacity cleared at the cap for three auctions ($333.44/MW-day for 2027/28, $325 for 2028/29) and 2027/28 was 6.6 GW short of the reliability requirement, so overrun days have never cost more.
ideas.wedge: Two frame families in one region (for example 7FA.03 and 7EA in PJM/MISO). First 10 customers: co-ops and municipal agencies with a 2027-28 hot-section outage coming, found through combustion-turbine users' groups and NRECA/APPA networks. Discount the first set in exchange for outage data.
ideas.path_to_100m: Revenue per swap outage about $6M (rent + usage reserves + guarantee) against a total event cost of $5-12M. $100M = about 17 outages a year = about 5% of roughly 350 US hot-section events a year (my derivation from 1,500-2,000 large frames and OEM intervals), or about 12% of the events at few-unit owners (heroic-adjacent; Canada, Mexico, Middle East extend it). Capital: sets cannot be shared across frame families, so 16-25 sets at $5-10M = $110-200M of assets. Analog: Willis Lease earned $291.6M lease rent and $232.0M maintenance-reserve revenue on roughly a $2.8B engine portfolio in 2025.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Multi-unit owners hold their own spares. OEMs run exchange and rotor programs inside LTSAs (GE rotor-in major inspection and seed-rotor concept, Siemens rotor exchange). ISPs offer repair-exchange (Chromalloy, Sulzer, EthosEnergy, Allied Power Group). For aeroderivatives, engine swaps are routine and ProEnergy sells repurposed jet cores. I found no neutral multi-owner pooled lease of frame hot-section sets in several searches.
ideas.why_they_lose: OEMs earn their margin on new parts and want LTSA lock-in, so they will not rent sets to non-LTSA owners. ISPs lack the balance sheet to leave $100M+ idle. Small owners cannot pool among themselves (frame mismatch, coordination). Neutrality plus cheap long-duration capital is the edge.
ideas.moat: Scale economies (each added customer lowers spares needed per customer), cornered resource (certified sets with serial-level records), switching costs (outage plans and records live with us), mild network effects (more owners raises the odds a compatible set is free).
ideas.earned_secret: The critical path of an outage is not labor, it is the shop-return slip, fixed when you booked the shop. Outages overrun mostly because repaired parts arrive late or the as-found scope grows and nobody holds a spare. Multi-unit fleets fix it privately with a seed rotor; the owners who need it most (one or two units) are exactly the ones who cannot afford it.
ideas.first_90_days: Weeks 1-3: 30 calls with outage managers and users' groups, map 2027-28 outage calendars by frame family. Weeks 4-8: LOIs for three spring-2027 outages, one repair partner signed, one infrastructure lender in talks. Weeks 9-12: buy or lease one used certified set via a broker, get an independent inspection, design the liquidated-damages wrap with an insurer. Key risk to test first: fit-up and interchangeability within a model.

ideas.title: Hot-Section Core Exchange (LKQ for turbines)
ideas.one_liner: Pay owners real money for retired hot-gas-path parts, give every part a serial-level remaining-life record, route them through partner repair shops, and sell warrantied remanufactured parts at 55-70% of OEM price.
ideas.customer: Non-LTSA owners buying parts per outage (merchant IPPs, co-ops, municipal agencies, cogens) and ISPs short of cores. Both sides of the exchange.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Outage manager or director of supply chain signs. Budget line: the outage parts line, which Turbomachinery calls the largest slice of maintenance spend. We also pay the owner a core credit, so the owner sees a net cut.
ideas.problem: There is no market price for retired cores. Owners get scrap value or an OEM/ISP trade-in credit set by the buyer. A repair vendor says components worth $7,600 as scrap were repaired for $1.3M and advises not to sell scrapped parts unseen (promotional, but the mechanism is real). Meanwhile new blades and vanes are the scarcest item in the industry.
ideas.solution: Core bid desk: the owner uploads its inspection report, gets a bid in 48 hours, is paid cash or credit. Each part gets a passport (serial, hours and starts, coatings, repair history, NDE). Partner shops repair to our spec for a fee. We own the inventory and sell reman sets with a one-year warranty backed by an insurer so lenders and insurers accept them. Cores feed the spare-set pool.
ideas.why_now: Casting scarcity makes every reusable airfoil precious (WoodMac, GE Aerospace-CPP deal). OEM service pricing is rising: GE Vernova says Q2 2026 growth came from higher volume and price, and transactional orders per unit keep rising by double digits. New units are 5-6 years out, so old frames run harder and longer.
ideas.wedge: 7FA.03 and 7EA families, where independents already repair and patents are long expired. First 10: owners outside OEM LTSAs, found through outage managers; collect their last three outages' disposition data to build the first core-price index.
ideas.path_to_100m: US cores: about 350 hot-section events a year (derived) x $2-4M repairable value = roughly $0.7-1.4B of cores a year. $100M of reman sales = about 25 sets at about $4M = about 7% of all US hot-section events, about 14% of events outside an OEM LTSA if half are. Heroic-adjacent in the US alone, so international ISP wholesale is part of the plan; globally about 6,000 large frames and this is under 2% of events. Gross margin 25-35%, so $25-35M gross profit.
ideas.who_does_it_today: ISPs buy cores for their own repair and exchange (Chromalloy, Sulzer, Liburdi, EthosEnergy under One Equity Partners, Allied Power Group under AEA Investors, MD&A). OEMs run exchange and trade-in programs. Brokers sell used parts (Turbologistics, World Wide Gas Turbine Products). Nobody found runs a neutral priced core exchange with serial-level passports.
ideas.why_they_lose: ISPs will not feed cores to rivals and want exclusivity. OEMs make their margin on new parts. Brokers lack engineering and certification.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (the core supply and its records), scale economies (batching repair capacity), data (remaining life by serial), network effects (more owners improves matching).
ideas.earned_secret: The aftermarket's scarce input is cores, not repair skill. A shop can always find a welder, it cannot always find a repairable bucket. Owners do not know what theirs is worth because nobody posts a price; whoever posts the price collects the supply.
ideas.first_90_days: Days 1-30: collect 20 anonymized retired-part dispositions from outage managers and publish a first core-value index. Days 31-60: two repair partners on rate cards. Days 61-90: buy the first five sets of cores and sell the first reman set to a co-op. Legal watch: LTSAs revert title to remaining parts life to the OEM, so stay on non-LTSA parts and out-of-patent designs.

ideas.title: Certified Unfired: the grading and escrow layer for stranded turbines and slot reservations (collectibles liquidity stack)
ideas.one_liner: A grading standard, escrow and OEM-consent layer so unfired and low-hour turbines, and later slot reservations, trade as a standardized asset: the PSA of turbines. The weakest idea of the 8: revenue is easy, a defensible profit pool is uncertain.
ideas.customer: Sellers: developers with stranded orders, utilities swapping units, reservation holders who cannot get power or permits. Buyers: data-center developers, utilities and industrials that cannot wait for 2030-31 OEM slots.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Buyer's VP power or head of energy procurement, CFO co-signs. Budget line: generation capex. WoodMac puts new turbines at about $600/kW by end-2027; Hallador paid about $760/kW for a 460 MW unfired Siemens package including generators and a steam turbine.
ideas.problem: The used-turbine market is fragmented, with no mandatory disclosure standards and no universal inspection protocol (per a seller's own description), and deposits can vanish. Buyers cannot verify preservation or whether the OEM will still warrant the unit. Hallador routed its units through Siemens USA refurbishment to keep OEM inspection and LTSA eligibility.
ideas.solution: A five-grade standard from unfired/OEM-refurbished/LTSA-eligible down to parts-only, with an independent inspection protocol and preservation records. Escrow and deposit protection, lien and title search, export-control screening, OEM refurbishment and consent orchestration, matching of transferable reservations where the OEM allows, and a principal desk for fast flips.
ideas.why_now: GE Vernova backlog plus reservations hit 116 GW with 2031 slots on sale; Siemens Energy's CEO says European buyers now pay reservation fees; turbine prices are up 195% since 2019 with roughly six-year lead times. Cleanview counts about 90 GW of behind-the-meter data-center power planned against about 2 GW operating, so many reservations and orders will fail to convert and need a buyer.
ideas.wedge: Hallador-style deals into US data-center developers. First 10: five stranded-unit sellers (the Energy World Corporation type) and five behind-the-meter buyers.
ideas.path_to_100m: Fee model: 3-4% of GMV needs $2.5-3.3B of trades a year, about 3.3-4.3 GW at $760/kW; that is heroic because only Hallador (0.46 GW) and ProEnergy (21 turbines, over 1 GW) are on record. Principal model: $100M of revenue is only about 130 MW a year but needs about $100M of inventory at 8-15% net margin ($8-15M). Honest verdict: easy gross revenue, thin and cyclical profit unless the grade becomes a gate lenders and OEMs recognize.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Turbologistics, World Wide Gas Turbine Products, USP&E Global, Surplus Record listings, ProEnergy (repurposed CF6 cores), older online-auction experiments (Enporion), OEM refurbishment arms (Siemens USA).
ideas.why_they_lose: Brokers have no grading, escrow or engineering. The OEM cannot be a neutral broker because it sells the scarce new slots, but it must consent to transfers; that consent is also the key dependency. If OEMs refuse, this idea is dead.
ideas.moat: A trusted standard accepted by lenders and insurers (branding), liquidity network effects, OEM-consent relationships (cornered resource). All three are weak until volume exists.
ideas.earned_secret: An unfired turbine's value is not its metal; it is whether the OEM will still warrant it and put it on an LTSA. Buyers cannot tell a properly preserved unit from one rusting in a crate, so the grade is the product.
ideas.first_90_days: Write the grading spec with two independent engineers and one OEM refurbishment contact. List three stranded units. Term-sheet one Hallador-style deal. Sign an escrow agent. Risk: a late-1990s speculative resale market in turbines on order collapsed with the cycle; this is the idea most exposed to an AI-capex pullback.

ideas.title: Outage Bench: a credentialed bench of turbine specialists (expert-labor marketplace plus spot labor)
ideas.one_liner: An employer-of-record bench of vetted ex-OEM technical advisors, Level-III inspectors, rotor and controls specialists and precision millwrights, with a published skills passport that insurers, owners and ISPs accept in place of an OEM badge, plus remote senior supervision. Weakest moat of the 8: a staffing business unless the credential becomes a standard.
ideas.customer: Outage managers; ISPs and EPCs with more outage work than people; OEM field arms at peak (GE's FieldCore, Mitsubishi Power).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Outage or plant manager; ISP VP operations. Budget line: outage labor.
ideas.problem: Combined Cycle Journal reports 80-90% of the experienced GE field engineers who commissioned the early-2000s fleet have left, while GE ramps output toward 30 GW a year. OEM technical advisors go to new-unit commissioning. Outage work is seasonal (one report: 35% of annual activity in the spring quarter, 15% in Q3), so craft idle between outages. OEM LTSAs typically require OEM-qualified supervision, so independent labor cannot easily touch covered scope.
ideas.solution: Recruit and retain 600-1,000 specialists as W-2 employees with per-diem and insurance. Publish a skills passport (work samples, OEM training history, incident record). A remote expert desk lets one Level-III supervise three to five crews on video. Pool the bench across owners to flatten seasonal peaks. Sell the credential to insurers and lenders.
ideas.why_now: OEM capacity is spoken for through 2031, outages cost more and run longer, and the workforce is aging with vocational pipelines drying up (GasTurbineHub, Equipment News).
ideas.wedge: Spring-2027 outages at non-LTSA units and ISP overflow. First 10: ten owners and two ISPs found through the same outage-manager network as the spare-set pool.
ideas.path_to_100m: US turbine-outage field labor is about $1.3B a year (derived: 350 hot-section events x $8M x 30% labor plus about 1,000 minor events x $1.2M x 40%). $100M of gross revenue = about 8% of that, about 4% if behind-the-meter and new-build commissioning labor is counted; about 700 people at roughly $140k billed per person-year. Take rate 18-25% means $18-25M gross profit, the thinnest margin of the 8.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Tradesmen International (reports about 988,000 outage man-hours), Nesfircroft, OEM field units, ISPs' own field forces (EthosEnergy calls itself the largest independent provider of field services), general staffing firms.
ideas.why_they_lose: OEMs staff only their own contracts and new-unit liquidated-damages work. Staffing firms have no credential and no supervision layer. ISPs hire only for themselves.
ideas.moat: Weak. A network of people (cornered resource) plus a passport and remote supervision (process power); switching costs are low. It becomes defensible only if insurers and OEM LTSAs accept the credential.
ideas.earned_secret: The binding constraint on third-party outage work is not bodies, it is a credential the OEM and insurer will accept. The know-how sits with a few thousand ex-OEM freelancers that owners cannot find.
ideas.first_90_days: Interview 25 outage managers, sign 50 freelance advisors, place three for spring 2027, and talk to two insurers about accepting the passport. Use W-2 employer-of-record to avoid worker-classification risk.

ideas.title: Progressive for Turbines: a condition-priced, insurer-backed independent LTSA
ideas.one_liner: A fixed-price per-hour maintenance contract for F- and E-class units priced on measured wear and operating history instead of the OEM's averaged equivalent-hours formula, with a pooled spare inventory and a reinsurer-backed parts-cost cap. It skims the best-run units the OEM formula overcharges.
ideas.customer: Owners whose OEM LTSAs expire in 2026-2029, or who pay transactional rates after expiry: co-ops, municipal agencies, PE-backed IPPs, industrials.
ideas.payer_and_signer: CFO and VP Generation sign; the lender's independent engineer for project-financed units. Budget line: LTSA fees, about $2-5M per large unit a year (derived from GMI's $4.5B US pool over about 1,500-2,000 units).
ideas.problem: OEM LTSAs price on equivalent operating hours, with the OEM defining how starts and trips convert to hours; the factors are fleet averages, so a clean baseload unit subsidizes a start-heavy one. LTSAs are close to non-terminable and trade sources say title to remaining life of parts bought under the contract reverts to the OEM. Older reporting says only OEMs offer LTSAs on F, G and H classes. Combined Cycle Journal notes that under an LTSA you may have no other option than hours-based overhauls. Scarcity has given OEMs pricing power.
ideas.solution: (1) A free forensic audit of the owner's LTSA (equivalent-hours math, true-up, title clauses). (2) A per-unit condition model from borescope, NDE and operating data (passport data from the core exchange). (3) A fixed $/hour price 10-20% under the OEM's for top-quartile units, with an annual true-up to measured condition, hedged by excess-of-loss reinsurance and pooled spares. (4) A delay and availability guarantee.
ideas.why_now: The 2000-2006 F-class fleet is rolling off contracts; OEM bandwidth is consumed by a 116 GW backlog; owners cannot escape to a replacement unit; casting scarcity makes a pooled-parts balance sheet valuable. Plant M&A at about $1,100/kW (LS Power paying about $5B for about 4.4 GW) means buyers now underwrite remaining life and capex closely.
ideas.wedge: Older-design frames where independents already have hardware (7FA.03, 501F, 7EA); third parties are weakest on directionally solidified and single-crystal blades on the newest machines, and Chromalloy advises OEM parts for designs under about 10 years old. First 10: co-ops and municipal agencies plus one PE-backed IPP, opened by the free audit.
ideas.path_to_100m: Revenue is contract fees. At $3-4M per F-class unit a year, $100M = 25-35 units = 2-3% of roughly 1,100 US baseload F-class units (derived), under 2% of all large frames. Share is not the constraint; credibility, bankability and balance sheet are. Gross margin 12-18% is my assumption (GE Vernova's Power segment ran an 18.8% EBITDA margin in Q2 2026 as a ceiling reference), so $12-18M gross profit. Global expansion available.
ideas.who_does_it_today: OEMs (GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, Mitsubishi Power); GE also runs cross-fleet service on rival 501F and SGT-800 machines, but through its own retrofit hardware as a conquest sale. Third-party term agreements exist: Wood Group has held a 7FA term service agreement with Associated Electric Cooperative, EthosEnergy has an eight-year Texas 7EA major-maintenance contract, and Allied Power Group and Sulzer do field service and repair. I found none offering condition-priced, reinsurer-backed F-class LTSAs.
ideas.why_they_lose: The OEM cannot price on condition without repricing its whole book: the good risks leave and it keeps the bad ones (adverse selection), and its hours formula is itself a profit lever. ISPs lack an insurance wrap and balance sheet. Insurers lack engineering.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning (OEMs cannot copy it without cannibalizing their book), data scale (the condition database improves pricing), switching costs (10-year contracts), cornered resource (the pool).
ideas.earned_secret: The real buyer of an LTSA is the lender's independent engineer, not the plant manager, and the equivalent-hours formula is an averaged price that anyone with better wear data can skim. The audit is the door; the takeout is the business.
ideas.first_90_days: Weeks 1-4: five free LTSA forensic reviews with co-ops and municipal agencies. Weeks 5-8: hire an ex-OEM contracts engineer and an ex-insurer engineering surveyor. Weeks 9-12: a term sheet from a specialty reinsurer for parts-cost excess-of-loss and a bid on one LTSA expiring in 2027. Legal: structure the guarantee through a licensed carrier and fronting arrangement, because regulators can treat guarantees as insurance (round 1's home-value-guarantee finalist died on this).

ideas.title: Hot-Section Repair Factory: automated multi-cycle repair the OEM would rather replace than do
ideas.one_liner: Two automated, permitted repair-and-coat shops that make second and third repairs routine on E- and F-class buckets, nozzles and shrouds, selling capacity to owners, ISPs and OEMs drowning in backlog.
ideas.customer: Non-LTSA owners, ISPs short of shop capacity, OEMs subcontracting overflow, and the core exchange.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Outage manager or supply-chain director; for the OEM channel, the VP service operations. Budget line: the repair line, which I estimate at about 22% of services, roughly $1B in the US (derived).
ideas.problem: Repair capacity (welding, coating, heat treatment, NDE) is manual and capacity-limited. OEMs designate parts life-limited and sell new, and put factory capacity on new units. With castings scarce, repair is the only airfoil supply for many owners. Permitting a coating and heat-treat facility takes years.
ideas.solution: Robotic laser cladding cells, scan-to-repair, adaptive machining, automated coating and NDE, and a qualified library of repair procedures per part number (using the ORNL/EPRI additive-repair route for hard-to-weld alloys). Sell through the core exchange. Start by acquiring a small permitted ISP shop and automating it.
ideas.why_now: The GE Aerospace-CPP deal and WoodMac make casting the industry's binding constraint; OEM transactional prices are rising by double digits per unit; old frames are being kept in service.
ideas.wedge: E-class and older F-class parts, where designs are old enough to be out of patent and ISPs already repair. First 10: owners plus one OEM overflow contract through the core exchange.
ideas.path_to_100m: Two shops at about $50M each. That is about 10% of a roughly $1B US repair market (derived) or under 2% of a roughly $6B global repair market (derived). Capital $40-60M per shop (assumption).
ideas.who_does_it_today: Chromalloy (repairs, coatings, castings), Sulzer, Liburdi (direct-energy-deposition repair), Allied Power Group (AEA Investors; bought EthosEnergy's generator division assets April 2026), EthosEnergy (One Equity Partners; bought TSL in 2025), MD&A, and OEM shops (GE has robotized arc-additive repair running in service centers). Howmet, PCC and CPP make new blades.
ideas.why_they_lose: The OEM earns more on replacement than repair and puts capacity on new units. The ISPs are PE-owned roll-ups with manual processes, spending on acquisitions rather than automation.
ideas.moat: Process power (qualified repair library and yields), cornered resource (permits and qualifications), scale economies.
ideas.earned_secret: Independents are limited by manual weld and re-qualification labor, not metallurgy. Automation plus a scan-to-repair library can make repeat repairs routine, which is exactly where OEM economics point the other way.
ideas.first_90_days: Identify two acquirable permitted shops, license a cladding cell, sign three owners and one ISP for first volumes, and start qualifying repair procedures on the top two part numbers. Legal: GE has stepped up legal action against copied parts, so do repair and out-of-patent designs, not new manufacture of newer ones; arrange insurer acceptance.

ideas.title: Megawatts from existing iron: financed, multi-vendor uprates paid from capacity revenue
ideas.one_liner: Packages of inlet cooling, controls and firing-temperature tuning, compressor and steam-path upgrades and supplemental firing, sold with financing and an accredited-MW guarantee. Weakest-evidenced of the 8: the uprate market must grow roughly 3-5x for it to work.
ideas.customer: IPPs and utilities with units in PJM, MISO, NYISO, ISO-NE and ERCOT.
ideas.payer_and_signer: SVP Asset Management or Commercial, with the CFO. Budget line: growth capex and merchant capacity revenue.
ideas.problem: At $325-333/MW-day a megawatt of accredited capacity earns about $119-122k a year, and a new turbine is 5-6 years out. Siemens Energy estimates up to about 6 GW from upgrading its own eligible US F-class units (vendor estimate). Real examples: Avista's Coyote Springs +18 MW, Consumers Energy's Zeeland +50 MW with a 2.5% efficiency gain. Yet PJM's 2028/29 auction cleared only 207.6 MW of uprates. OEMs sell upgrades as one-off hardware, tie them to LTSA renewals, and are short of engineering capacity.
ideas.solution: A multi-vendor integrator that buys hardware from the OEM or an ISP, adds controls tuning, M&V and ISO accreditation filings, finances the capex against contracted capacity revenue, and guarantees the accredited MW. Components: turbine inlet cooling (a vendor claims about $100/kW), controls tuning, compressor and steam-path upgrades, duct firing.
ideas.why_now: Capacity prices at the cap three auctions running, an RTO short of its reliability requirement, a 116 GW turbine backlog, and owners with no alternative. The 2026 PowerGen program carries a session on retrofit upgrades, so interest is real.
ideas.wedge: Hot-day derate recovery via inlet cooling and tuning on non-LTSA F-class units in PJM and MISO, where payback is one to two years. First 10: IPP fleets with summer capacity-performance exposure.
ideas.path_to_100m: About 400 MW a year of installed packages at about $250/kW (assumption) = $100M, about 2% a year of a roughly 20 GW US uprate potential (my extrapolation from Siemens' 6 GW for its own F-class). Revenue-share instead of turnkey is worse: 30% of $119k per MW-year needs about 2.8 GW installed. Heroic flag: PJM clears only about 200 MW of uprates per auction today, so we would be a large share of today's market.
ideas.who_does_it_today: GE Vernova (T-Fire and Advanced Gas Path upgrades), Siemens Energy, Mitsubishi Power, ISPs such as Power Systems Mfg and EthosEnergy, inlet-cooling vendors, and EPC firms.
ideas.why_they_lose: OEMs sell hardware up front and cannot take performance or financing risk across rival machines. Owners have capex hurdles and LTSA consent constraints.
ideas.moat: Weak to medium. Counter-positioning (multi-vendor, performance-guaranteed) and process power (M&V and accreditation expertise).
ideas.earned_secret: Every unit leaves megawatts on the table through hot-day lapse, conservative control margins and clearance degradation. With capacity at the cap an uprate pays back in one to two years, but nobody takes the performance risk and the financing.
ideas.first_90_days: Pick 20 non-LTSA F-class units in PJM and MISO, run hot-day performance screens, offer two owners a guaranteed-MW inlet-cooling and tuning package, and line up one capital partner. Legal watch: air-permit modification rules (an uprate that raises emissions can trigger major-source review), OEM approval under LTSAs, ISO accreditation rules.

ideas.title: Uptime Wrapper for mixed behind-the-meter data-center gas fleets
ideas.one_liner: Cross-OEM operations, maintenance and spares for AI-campus gas fleets built from whatever turbines and engines could be found: one contract, one uptime number for the whole site, with a pooled spare-engine inventory and a remote operations center.
ideas.customer: Behind-the-meter power developers and operators (neoclouds, Crusoe-type developers, power-as-a-service owners) and the infrastructure funds financing them.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Head of energy or COO of the developer; infrastructure-fund asset manager. Budget line: operating expense for energy supply plus lender-required reserves.
ideas.problem: Cleanview counts about 90 GW of behind-the-meter capacity planned and only about 2 GW operating, with xAI's Memphis sites (about 1.5 GW) most of it. Developers use whatever equipment is available (aeroderivatives, Solar Titans, recip engines, refurbished industrial turbines); Crusoe's Abilene site mixes LM2500XPRESS units with Solar Titan 350s. Each OEM guarantees only its own box and nobody guarantees the site.
ideas.solution: A site-level availability contract: operate (remote plus on-site), maintain across OEMs, hold pooled spare engines and parts for the common models, and schedule outages across the whole site. Priced per kW-year with availability credits.
ideas.why_now: About 12 GW of behind-the-meter gas and fuel-cell capacity tied to data-center projects had been announced by mid-2026 and owners have no choice but to run old and mixed equipment. OEMs are bundling service (Baker Hughes' deal with Kodiak includes training, spares and potential long-term services), which shows the budget exists and leaves the mixed-fleet case unserved.
ideas.wedge: Two or three mixed sites of 200-400 MW coming online in 2027. First 10: the 10-15 developers and funds with the largest announced behind-the-meter pipelines.
ideas.path_to_100m: All-in $80-100 per kW-year (assumption: aeroderivative parts-and-repair of about $6-10/MWh x 8,000 hours, plus operations labor and a risk premium). $100M = about 1.0-1.25 GW. Cleanview projects 5-13 GW operating by end-2027, so that is roughly 10-25% of operating capacity: heroic, and developers like Crusoe and VoltaGrid prefer to operate themselves. A smaller path is owning the spare-engine pool plus services.
ideas.who_does_it_today: OEMs with bundled service (Baker Hughes, Caterpillar, Solar Turbines, GE Vernova aeroderivative service), developers' in-house teams (Crusoe, xAI), VoltaGrid with Halliburton on a design-build-operate offering, Duos with Fortress operating mobile turbines, and ProEnergy on repurposed jet cores.
ideas.why_they_lose: Each OEM guarantees only its own equipment and has no incentive to take on a rival's engines. In-house teams lack bench depth and spares pools.
ideas.moat: Scale economies (pooled spares across customers), switching costs (embedded operations), cornered resource (cross-OEM runbooks and spare engines).
ideas.earned_secret: AI-campus power fleets are Frankenstein fleets, assembled from whatever could be bought. The customer's real KPI is cluster uptime, worth far more per megawatt-hour than a utility's wholesale power, so site-level uptime is the thing to sell and nobody can guarantee it today.
ideas.first_90_days: Interview 15 developers on their mixed-fleet maintenance plans, draft a site-level availability contract with a reinsurer, line up a pooled-engine supplier, and bid on one 2027 site. Air permitting stays the owner's risk, not ours (EPA reportedly found xAI's temporary Memphis turbines not exempt; that county permit expires 2027-01-02). Everything rides one capex cycle and behind-the-meter may be transitional once grid interconnection arrives.

ideas.title: Tooling Bank: custody and digital twins for every OEM-owned casting pattern, triggered by foundry closures
ideas.one_liner: Be the Iron Mountain for casting patterns: take custody of OEM-owned tooling before its foundry closes, scan it into a validated digital pattern, and become contractor of record when the part is re-sourced or printed.
ideas.customer: Mid-size and large OEMs that buy custom castings (valves, pumps, ag and construction, rail, mining, power), plus Navy/DLA programs with orphaned cast parts.
ideas.payer_and_signer: OEM VP/Director of Strategic Sourcing or Aftermarket Parts, from supplier-risk, tooling-management and aftermarket-spares budgets. Pays an annual custody fee, a one-time scan fee, and a casting margin when we route reorders. For DLA/Navy, the Land & Maritime engineering-support chain.
ideas.problem: OEMs own the patterns and core boxes but the tooling sits in a foundry's rafters; foundries often do not volunteer where it is stored (Casting Source columnist Charbauski, ex-foundry manager and OEM casting buyer, advises inventorying tooling and holding proof of ownership before a closure). Closures keep happening (Dalton/First Brands, Neenah Lincoln, Smith Foundry via EPA settlement, Friends Foundry). Each lost pattern means a new pattern, requalification and months of delay (BCG: 6-18+ months to cast or forge a part).
ideas.solution: (1) Closure-triggered rescue: find foundries 3-9 months from closing (WARN notices, air-permit surrenders, trade press) and call their customers. (2) Custody: retrieve, inventory, tag, store, document chain of ownership. (3) Digitize: 3D scan plus CAD reconstruction plus gating record, validated by a sample casting. (4) Route: when a pattern is lost or a foundry is slow, print the sand mold and run first article at a partner foundry, then handle reorders as contractor of record. (5) Registry: live map of every tool, owner, location and condition.
ideas.why_now: Foundry closures; the DoW plan (2026-09-30) names qualification delays; DLA funded a printed-sand pilot for obsolete critical castings ($15M potential, option exercised May 2025, with ExOne/Desktop Metal and CTC); Humtown runs a sand-printing fleet in Ohio; sand printing makes the pattern a file.
ideas.wedge: A 'Closure Response Kit' priced per tool (about $2.5k scan plus $250 a year custody), sold to OEMs that buy from a foundry that just filed a WARN notice. First 10: mid-size valve, pump, ag and rail OEMs that are customers of the next 5 closing foundries; DLA's MetaL FACT team as a referral channel.
ideas.path_to_100m: I could not find a count of OEM-owned patterns, so this rests on my assumptions. AFS counts about 1,956 metalcasting facilities (2018). Assume about 2,000 OEM-owned sets per foundry, so about 3.9M sets. At maturity: custody/registry at $250 a set a year on 300k sets (about 8% of all sets) is $75M; digitizing 12k sets a year at $2.5k is $30M; routing 4k re-sourced sets a year at $25k annual casting spend each is $100M of castings (about $15M margin if booked net). Total about $120M if castings are booked as principal, about $50M if net. Needs about 8% of US OEM-owned tooling; verify the pattern count first.
ideas.who_does_it_today: DLA's DECAF and ICON databases (ICON includes a cast tooling database and supplier database; free, DLA-managed NSNs only, no custody, no casting); DLA MetaL FACT and AFCAT (free); OEM spreadsheets and generic ERP tooling modules; Casting Source advice; Humtown and ExOne/Desktop Metal (sand printing, via the CTC/DLA pilot); Xometry and Fictiv run their own networks. I found no startup doing custody plus digital twin plus routing.
ideas.why_they_lose: DLA's tools cover only DLA-managed NSNs and neither hold tooling nor cast parts. Foundries have no incentive to help customers leave. Print bureaus sell molds, not custody and qualification. OEM systems track assets they hold, not tooling at suppliers.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (physical custody, chain-of-ownership proof, a validated twin accepted in the OEM's quality system) and switching costs (changing vault means revalidating).
ideas.earned_secret: The pattern, not the foundry, is the real lock-in, and the OEM usually does not know where it is. The rescue window is months before the doors close; once a lender or auctioneer controls the building, ownership paperwork decides who gets the patterns. Procurement does not know this; pattern-shop managers and foundry owners do. Legal premise to check: some states give a possessory lien on customer tooling (Illinois Tool and Die Lien Act covers patterns, subordinate to perfected UCC Article 9 interests; Michigan MCL 445.618; Arizona), so OEMs should file UCC statements and mark tools; scans of defense parts are ITAR/CUI.
ideas.first_90_days: Weeks 1-3: list every foundry closing in the next 12 months and interview 10 owners. Weeks 3-8: offer 3 OEMs a free audit of tooling at their top 5 foundries. Weeks 8-12: take custody of the first 200 tools, scan 30, print one mold and pour a sample. Kill test: if fewer than 3 of 10 OEMs will pay $250 per tool per year or accept routing, shrink or drop.

ideas.title: Second-Source Factory: sell approved part numbers, not consulting hours
ideas.one_liner: A fixed-price factory that turns a sole-sourced or backordered casting into two prime-approved sources, where the approval package and the process data are the product.
ideas.customer: Aerospace, defense, shipbuilding and energy primes and tier-1s with sole-sourced or long-backordered cast parts; Navy submarine-base suppliers; DLA.
ideas.payer_and_signer: VP Supply Chain or Director of Supplier Development at the prime, or the program supplier-readiness budget (a Navy official cited $605M of supplier-development money in the FY24 supplemental, routed via BlueForge Alliance). Priced per approved part number.
ideas.problem: Castings and forgings are 3% of DLA NSNs but 20% of its 100 oldest backorders (DLA, NDIA 2024). Lead times are 6-18+ months and OEMs cannot see below tier-1 (BCG). Second-sourcing is nobody's job: SQEs are overloaded, each prime has its own package, and a 60-person foundry cannot write one. The DoW plan blames qualification delays and poor understanding of process variables.
ideas.solution: A qualification line: ingest drawing and spec; pick two candidate foundries from a capability graph; simulate gating and solidification; make tooling (printed molds where possible); pour a sample lot; CT or X-ray; run AS9102 first article and the prime-specific forms; shepherd through the prime's SQE and DCMA/NAVSEA gate; hand over a source with a process-fingerprint record. Keep it alive with annual change control (subscription). The registry of approved positions by part number becomes the format primes ask for.
ideas.why_now: DoW plan; GE-CPP shows engine makers scrambling for capacity; Navy sub base needs supplier-provided material to grow over 200% for Virginia and Columbia; BlueForge holds a sole-source contract up to $980.7M; simulation, CT and sand printing cut cycle time.
ideas.wedge: Navy and DLA backordered or orphaned castings. First 10: tier-1 valve, pump and piping assemblers on Virginia/Columbia supply chains, plus DLA L&M referrals. Ten part numbers at a fixed fee.
ideas.path_to_100m: No public benchmark exists for the cost of qualifying a second casting source; assume $75k average per approved part number (my assumption). Year 6: 800 approvals a year is $60M, plus a maintenance subscription of $10k a year on 4,000 live part numbers is $40M, so $100M. Needs about 150 buyer organizations with about 5-6 part numbers a year each, outsourcing the work. Funding pool evidence: BlueForge's $605M supplier-development line in one supplemental. The assumption to test is that primes will outsource it.
ideas.who_does_it_today: In-house supplier-development and SQE teams (Anduril is hiring casting SQE and industrialization roles; Hadrian is hiring casting engineers); DLA MetaL FACT and AFCAT (free for DLA NSNs); American Metalcasting Consortium (DLA ManTech-funded projects); Cetim (France) qualification service; BCG-style advisors; low-cost-country sourcing agents; Xometry and Fictiv for commercial parts; BlueForge pays for supplier readiness.
ideas.why_they_lose: In-house teams cannot scale to the backlog. DLA and the consortium serve DLA NSNs and pilots, not prime production. Consultants sell hours and carry no approval risk. Marketplaces avoid flight-critical and SUBSAFE parts.
ideas.moat: Process power (a repeatable qualification line), cornered resource (approved positions and data on which foundries pass first time), and a registry format that becomes the standard primes request.
ideas.earned_secret: Second-sourcing a casting is rarely a metallurgy problem. It is a sequencing-and-paperwork problem that nobody owns: tooling, sample lot, CT, first article and prime-specific forms sit in six different hands, and a small foundry cannot write a prime's package. The SQE's real job is chasing those pieces.
ideas.first_90_days: Pick 10 part numbers with documented backorders (DLA DIBBS, Navy) and approach the holders with a fixed fee, 50% payable on approval. Run two end to end at a partner foundry. Build the form library for 3 primes. Kill test: if no prime accepts a third-party package at the same gate, this collapses into consulting and is dead.

ideas.title: Tier-Three Credit: lend against the prime's payment and the customer's tooling, not the foundry's balance sheet
ideas.one_liner: Multi-tier supply chain finance for defense and aerospace foundries and machine shops, repaid by sweeping the prime's payment so the borrower's weak credit matters little.
ideas.customer: Foundries, forges and machine shops that are tier-2 or tier-3 on prime programs. The sponsor is a prime or tier-1 that does not want capacity to fail.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The borrower (foundry owner or CFO) pays about 10-14% all-in. The prime's VP Supply Chain signs a payment-direction program that costs them nothing and supports their resilience goals.
ideas.problem: The DoW plan describes a 'financing impasse' where investors wait for firm customer commitments and customers wait for proven product. J.P. Morgan and others say access to finance deteriorates sharply below tier-1. OSC loans run $10M-$150M and fund plant and equipment, not working capital. A $2M order can need $1.2M of metal, pattern repair and payroll up front and pay 90 days after the machine shop approves.
ideas.solution: Pattern transplant of 'control the repayment channel' (payroll deduction or wallet sweep). The prime or tier-1 signs a payment direction for named POs. The platform advances up to 60-70% of PO value at acceptance (Twinco does this for retailers), then lends against WIP and finished inventory, collects from the prime into a controlled account, takes a security interest in receivables and, where the OEM agrees, in OEM-owned tooling. DPAS rating and prime acceptance history are underwriting signals.
ideas.why_now: DoW plan; Navy submarine-base buildout; the FY27 request seeks about $20.2B for the Defense Strategic Capital Credit Program but lends at $10M+ for capex; banks are publishing defense working-capital playbooks; castings backlogs.
ideas.wedge: 10 foundries on one prime's Navy program, a $10-20M warehouse line from a credit fund, and one prime or tier-1 signing the program.
ideas.path_to_100m: At about 12% all-in yield, $100M of revenue needs about $830M average outstanding, or about 280 borrowers at $3M. Assume working capital is 15-20% of casting revenue (my assumption), so $8-11B is tied up in US castings; $830M is 8-10% of that. Net revenue after about 6-7% cost of funds is roughly half, so the revenue test passes and the profit test needs about twice the book. Needs a $1B+ debt facility.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Prime-anchored supply chain finance (Taulia, C2FO, PrimeRevenue, from memory; tier-1 invoices); J.P. Morgan and Citi defense inventory and receivables finance; PO-finance shops (King Trade Capital, Wells Fargo PO Finance Group, SouthStar; $150k-$5M deals); Twinco (retail); OSC; SBA; ABL lenders. I found no defense-casting specialist.
ideas.why_they_lose: Anchor programs fund only invoices the anchor approves, which means tier-1. PO lenders price the borrower, not the prime. OSC funds capex. Nobody lends against customer-owned tooling plus rated orders.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning against banks; scale economies in funding (more primes signed means lower losses and cheaper capital); switching costs once embedded in a prime's AP.
ideas.earned_secret: Foundries rarely die from lack of orders. They die in the gap between buying metal and payroll for a $2M order and getting paid 90 days after the machine shop approves. Bankers underwrite the foundry; the right underwriting is the prime's payment and the part's quality acceptance history.
ideas.first_90_days: Find one prime or tier-1 sponsor (a Navy valve or pump OEM) willing to sign payment direction for 10 named suppliers. Line up a $10M credit-fund facility. Fund the first 3 POs. Check UCC Article 9 treatment of anti-assignment clauses (my recollection: it generally overrides them for accounts) and state lender licensing with counsel. Kill test: if no prime will sign payment direction, it is just PO finance at a worse price.

ideas.title: Foundry BOT: build, staff, operate and transfer foundries for the new buyers who cannot hire the people
ideas.one_liner: Fluor plus an operating team for foundries: design, power, permit, commission and run a plant for 3 years, then hand it over, so buyers with money and no casting people get capacity in about 24 months.
ideas.customer: Neo-primes and OEMs deciding to build casting capacity: SpaceX (Bastrop blade foundry), Hadrian, Anduril, GE after CPP, Safran (Rennes), Navy submarine-base suppliers.
ideas.payer_and_signer: COO, VP Manufacturing or Chief Supply Chain Officer. Capex for design-build, opex for an operating fee.
ideas.problem: BCG: rebuilding experienced engineering expertise takes 5-10 years and training new production staff 3-6 months. New US foundries cost $100M+. Power and permits, not construction, set the schedule: A.Y. McDonald's nine-figure Wisconsin foundry waited on a 10-mile transmission line; SpaceX's Bastrop permits are pending. Equipment (induction furnaces, sand systems, heat treat, NDT) comes from separate vendors.
ideas.solution: Standard modular foundry designs by process (steel sand, investment, aluminum). Site selection starts from power and air-permit availability, favoring shuttered foundry sites. Reserve long-lead equipment slots. A commissioning bench of retired and mid-career foundry GMs, metallurgists, melt supervisors and NDT leads. A 36-month operating contract with a yield incentive, then transfer, with an option to co-own.
ideas.why_now: Cluster of builds: Pratt Asheville ($650M by 2027), Howmet Wichita Falls ($70M), Doncasters Bochum ($52M), Safran Rennes, Ford Meter Box (290,000 sq ft), SpaceX Bastrop (336 ha), Fabri's one-foundry-a-year plan. GE's $11.75B CPP deal shows buyers pay for capacity; the DoW plan says there is no latent capacity.
ideas.wedge: A fixed-fee 12-week 'foundry readiness' study (power, air-permit path, equipment slots, staffing plan) offered to 10 neo-primes and OEMs, converting to design-build.
ideas.path_to_100m: Assume 25 US foundry projects over 5 years averaging $120M, so $3B of capex (my estimate; named projects above exceed $1B). Gross design-build revenue of $100M a year is about 17% share of that. Add an operating fee of 4% of plant revenue on 5 plants of $100M, so $20M. Net fees are only about 10-25% of that gross, so this is a services wedge; the scaling assets are standard designs, reserved equipment slots, a permitted-site bank and co-ownership stakes.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Equipment OEMs (Inductotherm, ABP, ALD, Disa, Sinto, Kuttner, from memory) sell machines and sometimes lines; general contractors; EPC majors (Fluor, Jacobs) that do not operate foundries; in-house teams at Howmet, CPP and Pratt; Fabri builds its own; BCG advises only.
ideas.why_they_lose: Equipment vendors carry no schedule or yield risk and do not staff. EPCs do not know melting. In-house teams compete for the same scarce experts.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (the operator bench, equipment slots, permitted sites) and process power (standard designs).
ideas.earned_secret: A foundry's schedule is set by the utility and the air permit. Its success depends on about 20 people (melt supervisor, metallurgist, core-room lead, heat-treat lead, NDT Level III) who each took 15 years to make. Buyers think they are buying equipment; they are buying those people.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign 3 readiness studies. Recruit a 10-person advisory bench of retired foundry GMs. Map 20 shuttered foundry sites with live air permits and grid service. Kill test: if every neo-prime hires its own team, drop the services and keep only the permitted-site bank.

ideas.title: The Non-GE Foundry: customer-funded independent castings capacity for everyone who just lost a neutral supplier
ideas.one_liner: A neutral investment and structural casting platform financed by 10-year take-or-pay contracts from the engine, turbine and defense makers who cannot buy a CPP and do not want to depend on a competitor's captive.
ideas.customer: Non-captive buyers of airfoils and structural castings: industrial gas-turbine makers other than GE, engine and airframe makers without in-house foundries, Navy primes. I did not verify which companies buy from CPP.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Chief Procurement Officer or VP Supply Chain signs a 10-year take-or-pay (BCG recommends 10+ years versus today's 5-7); CFO signs prepayments.
ideas.problem: GE agreed to buy CPP for $11.75B (about $2.0B 2027 revenue, about 26x EBITDA). Howmet fell about 10% on in-sourcing fears. SpaceX is building its own blade foundry. TechCrunch reports four casters at industrial scale, all at capacity. GE Vernova is taking slot reservations for 2031 (116 GW backlog). A Vertical Research analyst said it remains to be seen whether the deal affects CPP's non-GE customers. Non-captive buyers are price-takers in a queue.
ideas.solution: Build or buy-and-expand an independent caster at about $100M of revenue per plant, starting with one hard niche where non-captive buyers share a design (for example one frame size of turbine vanes). Fund it with a buyer consortium's take-or-pay and prepayments plus project debt (OSC capex loans of $10M-$150M, infrastructure credit). Offer open-book cost-plus pricing and a no-captive policy (no engine business). Run in-plant CT and a process-data record per casting.
ideas.why_now: GE-CPP (2026-09-08), SpaceX Bastrop, the DoW plan, the Doncasters IPO ($919M, June 2026), the OSC FY27 request, and Wood Mackenzie's 60-70 GW a year capacity against about 110 GW of orders.
ideas.wedge: One product family and one modest first plant, or a distressed qualified foundry as the nucleus. First 10: signed capacity LOIs from non-captive buyers.
ideas.path_to_100m: CPP's roughly $2.0B across more than 20 facilities is about $100M per facility (my arithmetic), so $100M equals one CPP-average plant. At CPP's price-to-revenue of about 5.9x ($11.75B over $2.0B), a $100M plant is worth about $590M if the multiple holds. Capital need is my estimate of $150-300M per plant (a new US foundry is reported at over $100M; Pratt's integrated Asheville is $650M). The pool share is tiny; the binding constraints are capital and a 3-5 year qualification path.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Howmet; CPP (becoming GE-owned); Doncasters (public since June 2026); Chromalloy; ATI; PCC Airfoils; RTX/Pratt, Safran and SpaceX (captive); Fabri (small investment casting, shipping to Lockheed and RTX); Hadrian (in-house plans). Pursuit Aerospace bought Creasey Castings on 2026-08-11 (roll-up).
ideas.why_they_lose: Dilemma: every incumbent allocates scarce capacity to its highest-priority long-term agreements and cannot give rivals dedicated, open-book capacity without destroying its pricing power. CPP's new owner competes with CPP's other customers. Captive builders serve only themselves.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (qualified capacity under long-term contract), switching costs, scale economies, and counter-positioning (neutrality as the feature).
ideas.earned_secret: Castings capacity goes to whoever is strategically closest to the supplier's owner. When your supplier becomes a competitor's subsidiary, you do not need a cheaper source, you need a neutral one whose capacity is contractually yours. Hypothesis to test: buyers will prefund it because dedicated capacity is worth more to them than the price premium.
ideas.first_90_days: Talk to 15 procurement heads at non-captive buyers to test willingness to sign a 10-year take-or-pay. Recruit two ex-Howmet or ex-PCC plant leaders. Identify 3 distressed qualified foundries as acquisition nuclei. Kill test: if no buyer will prepay, the capital stack does not close and the idea is dead.

ideas.title: One Approved Supplier, Two Hundred Foundries: the supplier of record that CT-screens before machining and guarantees good parts
ideas.one_liner: A prime-approved supplier of record that buys rough castings from a vetted network, CT-screens them before machining, machines them, and ships finished parts at a guaranteed-good-part price, carrying the yield risk nobody else will.
ideas.customer: OEMs and primes buying machined cast parts (valves, pumps, vehicles, rail, heavy equipment, Navy components) who manage 5-20 foundries and shops per part family.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Director or VP Supply Chain, from the direct materials budget. Pays a finished-part price at an assumed 5-12% premium over piece price for the guarantee.
ideas.problem: Defects surface late: one investment-casting plant reports 99.9% of returns are defects found in machining. Foundries lose at least 5% of revenue to scrap and rework (Swansea). Primes cannot onboard and police hundreds of tiny suppliers. Shops charge for machining scrap and disputes follow.
ideas.solution: One approved supplier for the finished part. Qualify and audit foundries once, not per customer. CT or X-ray before machining. Machine in network or in own cells. Ship with a data package. Price per good part. Use the process-to-defect-to-machining-outcome data to steer each part to the foundry and process with the best predicted yield. Grow by buying a closing foundry's customer book when its approvals can be moved (the Lacy Foundries pattern).
ideas.why_now: Lumafield launched a large-format CT scanner (Saturn, 2026-09-10); the DoW plan calls for advanced inspection and process monitoring; capacity is short; neo-primes such as Hadrian are moving into casting. I did not rely on CMMC (Phase 2 was suspended 2026-07-13).
ideas.wedge: Commercial-grade heavy-equipment, valve and pump castings where CT screening is contractual. First 10: mid-size OEMs with open scrap disputes, then Navy tier-1s.
ideas.path_to_100m: Revenue is finished-part sales: 40 customers at $2.5M is $100M, only about 0.19% of the $53.7B pool. Target gross margin 18-25% after scrap risk. Demand proof: Xometry's marketplace did $205M in Q1 2026 (castings not broken out).
ideas.who_does_it_today: Xometry and Fictiv (networks, no yield guarantee, strongest in prototypes and low volume); CASTFAST (Germany, 30 foundries); Sourcing Planet/SUpplyDU (Europe); AFS's free supplier finder; vertically integrated foundry-machining houses (from memory); contract machine shops; Hadrian (CNC, adding casting).
ideas.why_they_lose: Dilemma: marketplaces take no risk and avoid critical parts; machine shops are paid by the hour and cannot carry casting yield risk; foundries lack CT, machining and capital; primes' ERPs track price and delivery, not per-casting risk.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning against marketplaces (we carry the risk), a data asset (process, defect, machining outcome), and scale economies in CT.
ideas.earned_secret: Nobody owns the seam between the foundry and the machine shop, and that is where the money disappears: porosity is invisible until a tool breaks through it after hours of machining. Whoever puts the CT gate before the machine and owns both sides' cost wins the argument and the data.
ideas.first_90_days: Find 5 OEMs with documented scrap-dispute costs on machined castings. Rent CT time at a service bureau. Run 3 part families end to end with two foundries and a shop. Get product-liability and E&O insurance quotes. Kill test: if gross margin after scrap is under 12% on the pilots, the guarantee is mispriced.

ideas.title: US-Pour: the verified melt-and-pour ledger that turns 'made from US steel' into a 25-to-40-point tariff cut
ideas.one_liner: The compliance rail for the April 2026 Section 232 rule that taxes steel derivatives made entirely from US-melted-and-poured steel at 10% instead of 25-50%: heat-level attestations from foundries and mills, audit-ready for CBP.
ideas.customer: Importers of record of cast and steel derivative goods (valves, fittings, pumps, components), foreign contract assemblers in Mexico, Canada and Korea that use US castings, and US foundries and mills selling 'US-poured' content.
ideas.payer_and_signer: VP Trade Compliance or Chief Procurement Officer at the importer (budget: duty cost); foundry sales VP for the sell-side credential. Price about 1% of entered value or per attestation.
ideas.problem: Since 2026-04-06, Section 232 applies to full customs value, with tiers of 50%, 25% and 15% and 10% for articles made entirely from US-melted-and-poured steel; importers need enhanced melt-and-pour documentation. Mill certificates are PDFs with no standard layout, heat numbers get mistranscribed, the exemption is all-or-nothing per article (per a commercial source), and EY and Perkins Coie disagree on 'entirely' versus at least 95%.
ideas.solution: A heat-lot ledger binding mill and foundry melt records (heat number, chemistry, date, facility) to downstream lots, parts and shipments. It issues entry-ready attestation packages (US-content claim code plus certificates for CBP's ACE document system), spot-audits suppliers, and insures the claim. The same ledger serves DFARS specialty-metals and Build America, Buy America iron-and-steel proofs.
ideas.why_now: The 2026-04-02 proclamation (effective 2026-04-06); melt-and-pour reporting since 2024-11-21; the FY2026 NDAA reportedly names castings and forgings as priority components; tariff exposure is now a board-level cost.
ideas.wedge: US foundries and mills that ship castings or bar to Mexican, Canadian and Korean assemblers, and the importers that re-import the derivative. First 10: 5 foundries and 5 valve, pump or fittings importers.
ideas.path_to_100m: The Feb 2025 derivative list covers about $150B of 2024 imports; core steel and aluminum imports were $25B and $18B in 2025 (CRS). At 1% of entered value, $100M needs $10B through the rail, about 6.7% of the $150B list. For an importer, 25% to 10% on $10B saves about $1.5B a year (the fee is about 7% of savings); at the 50% tier it saves $4B. This is heroic share and rests on how much of the list can be made entirely from US-melted steel, which is unknown.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Customs brokers and trade-compliance software (Descartes, Thomson Reuters ONESOURCE, Flexport, Zonos, Avalara) handle classification and duty math; mill-certificate extraction and traceability vendors (Algoscale DocumentIQ, Oxmaint, Kissflow, Assent); importer spreadsheets; mills' own certificates. I found no heat-level, foundry-native attestation product tied to the 10% rate.
ideas.why_they_lose: Broker software works at the HTS and invoice level and treats mill certificates as attachments. Mills and foundries do not want liability for importers' claims. Importers' ERPs do not hold heat numbers.
ideas.moat: Network effects (more melters on the ledger means more eligible content), cornered resource (verified melt records and audit history), and switching costs.
ideas.earned_secret: For a foundry, 'melted and poured' is an event it controls and records, and the heat number is the only thing that survives from furnace to ship; it is mistranscribed all the time. The ledger is a data-integrity problem that the foundry is uniquely placed to solve. Main risk is legal and policy: the exact 'entirely' test, CBP guidance (a commercial source cites CSMS 68253075; verify it), whether supplier attestation alone suffices, false-claim liability, and no customs-broker activity without a license. The Annex III reduced framework expires 2027-12-31 and litigation is pending, so the rule can change or vanish.
ideas.first_90_days: Read the proclamation, annexes and CBP guidance with a customs attorney. Interview 10 importers and 5 foundries. Prototype a ledger on 3 foundry heat records, ending in an entry-ready package. Kill test: if CBP accepts a plain supplier attestation, or the 10% preference is dropped, pivot to audit insurance or drop.

ideas.title: Cleaning Room as a Service: we run the foundry's finishing department and bill per casting
ideas.one_liner: Take over the department foundries cannot staff: robotic grinding, cut-off and weld-repair cells plus trained operators inside the foundry's building, billed per casting finished with a guaranteed cost ceiling.
ideas.customer: Mid-size steel, iron and nonferrous foundries (100-500 employees) with high-mix, medium-to-large castings still ground by hand; later primes' captive foundries.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Foundry owner, GM or VP Operations, from the cleaning-room labor and abrasives budget.
ideas.problem: Cleaning and finishing are 20-35% of manufacturing cost of an average casting (Foundry Magazine) and the cleaning room has the highest turnover in the foundry (Swedish study). A defense foundry found its cleaning room was the bottleneck and could not hire operators. A Pentagon official is quoted saying 122,000 more cast-and-forge workers are needed by 2028 (date unclear). Robot vendors sell capex projects with per-part programming; Eagle Alloy found them aimed at high-volume work and built its own cell.
ideas.solution: An outsourced in-plant department. Scan-to-path uses the foundry's own gating and method file, since cut-off points are known before the pour. Force-controlled grinding and cut-off cells, CT-guided weld repair later, operators on our payroll. Per-casting or per-pound pricing with a guaranteed ceiling below current cost. We own the robots and the recipe library.
ideas.why_now: Labor shock; the DoW plan; vision-first grinding robots (Pivot Robotics, YC W24) show feasibility; Benton Foundry reports two operators replacing seven grinders (vendor-reported).
ideas.wedge: Steel foundries with Navy or defense backlog whose cleaning room is the bottleneck; 3 pilot cells.
ideas.path_to_100m: Assume manufacturing cost is about 90% of $53.7B and cleaning is the low-end 20%, so about $9.7B a year (my assumption). Addressable high-mix medium and large castings are about 30%, so about $2.9B. $100M is about 3.4% of the addressable fee pool, or about 1% of all cleaning spend. In cells, at about $250k a cell-year (replacing about 5 FTEs plus abrasives), that is about 400 cells.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Integrators and vendors (Weiler, Vulcan Engineering, Barinder, ABB, Fanuc); foundry self-builds (Eagle Alloy, Benton); Pivot Robotics (funding unclear); Path Robotics for welding (from memory); staffing agencies; offshoring. I found no per-casting managed-service player.
ideas.why_they_lose: Integrators sell capex and leave. Foundries lack robot programmers. Staffing firms cannot fix turnover.
ideas.moat: Process power (recipe library keyed to pattern and method), switching costs (in-plant), and purchasing scale. This is the weakest moat of the eight.
ideas.earned_secret: Cleaning-room robots failed because every cast shape varies, but the foundry already holds the answer: gate and riser positions are in the method file and solidification model, and the pattern is fixed. It is a data-integration problem more than a robotics problem. Legal premise to check: collective-bargaining subcontracting clauses (many foundries are unionized) and dust, noise and workplace-safety liability.
ideas.first_90_days: Visit 10 foundries and record cleaning-room cost per casting. Sign 3 pilots on one casting family each. Build the scan-to-path loop from one method file to one finished casting. Kill test: if the cell cannot beat manual cost per casting by 25% on 3 families, drop.

ideas.title: Harvest Pit Crew
ideas.one_liner: A per-machine, per-season uptime subscription for custom harvesters and big grain farms: winter inspection, parts caches and roving techs staged along the northbound harvest route, a loaner combine, and a 24-hour-or-credit promise on the older, mixed-brand machines the OEM uptime programs exclude.
ideas.customer: Interstate custom harvesting crews (typically 4-10 combines each) and Plains grain farms running two or more combines with no real shop of their own.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The crew owner, or the farm owner/operations manager, signs. Paid from repairs-and-maintenance and custom-hire/rental lines, priced per machine-season (my estimate $12-18k, against custom combining rates near $25-30/acre and about $46/acre total cost for combine plus header per Nebraska Extension). A lender can fold it into the operating note.
ideas.problem: A combine down in the one dry window costs more than the repair invoice. OEM answers are narrow: Deere JD Protect gives a 24-hour uptime assurance (rental machine) only on new X/S-Series combines and only if every maintenance event is done at the dealer; AGCO Harvest Promise is a European parts-delay refund; Gleaner and Fendt programs are dealer-bound. Older and mixed-brand fleets have no service level, and dealers cannot promise one: in a Sept 2023 poll 65% of dealers expected losses above 9% of revenue from unfilled technician jobs.
ideas.solution: Seasonal contract per machine: (1) winter inspection and baseline; (2) predicted-failure parts caches by model and hours in 4-6 depots along the Texas-to-Canada route; (3) two-person roving tech teams with dealer-equivalent tools (Deere PRO Service, reported at $195 per machine, plus a multi-brand Jaltest-class tool at roughly $4-7k); (4) a loaner/rental combine pool; (5) a service credit if a machine is not cutting within 24 hours of a call. Year two adds sprayer and planter seasons so techs and depots earn year-round. Failure data keyed by serial becomes the underwriting asset for open-network coverage.
ideas.why_now: Deere's July 8, 2026 FTC/five-state settlement requires dealer-equivalent repair resources for farmers and independents for 10 years (pending court approval), and PRO Service has allowed owner-permissioned reprogramming since July 2025, so non-dealer techs can work on electronics-heavy combines. EPA said in Feb 2026 that farmers and independents may repair DEF systems. Deere expects North American ag equipment sales down another 15-20% in 2026, so crews run older machines longer. AGCO's FarmerCore proves farmers want on-farm service, but only inside the dealer.
ideas.wedge: Winter 2026-27: inspect 40-60 combines for 8-10 custom crews in KS/NE/SD, hire 6 ex-dealer techs, open one Kansas depot. First run starting June 2027 on about 100 machine-seasons. First ten customers: crew chiefs reached through the custom-harvester association network and the elevators crews work with.
ideas.path_to_100m: 6,000 combine-seasons x about $16.5k = $99M. That is roughly 6-9% of an estimated 70-100k combines under 15 years old (my estimate from unit sales: about 3,579 US combines sold in 2025 per a secondary reading of farmdoc data; Power Systems Research ~7,100 North American units built in 2023; not a census count). Custom crews alone likely cap near $60-70M (my estimate of ~4,000 crew combines; the only national crew count I found is 3,431 crews in 1971), so the rest must come from farms plus a spring season on sprayers and tractors. Revenue is gross billings at roughly 25-30% gross margin (my estimate). The upper end needs heroic share.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Deere JD Protect (24h uptime assurance, new X/S combines, dealer maintenance required); AGCO Harvest Promise (EU), GleanerCare, Fendt Gold Star; dealer pre-harvest packages (e.g., Greenway); RDO Ready+; AGCO FarmerCore mobile trucks; crews' own mechanics and chase trucks; scattered independent mobile mechanics. I found no brand-agnostic, route-based uptime service.
ideas.why_they_lose: A dealer sits at a fixed address inside a franchise territory, earns about 61.5% gross margin on service hours (Titan FY2026) largely from breakdowns, cannot service the red combine and the green tractor under one contract, and cannot hire the techs to staff a roaming bench. A per-season uptime contract pays them less when machines break less.
ideas.moat: Scale economies in route density (one parts cache and tech team amortized over many machines) plus counter-positioning against fixed-site, hours-billed dealer service.
ideas.earned_secret: A custom crew's profit is cutting hours, not repair cost per hour, and its own mechanics already fix most problems; what they lack is the right part at 9 p.m. in a town with no dealer, and a second pair of hands. The route is predictable (Texas/Oklahoma wheat late May, Kansas in June, Nebraska and the Dakotas into Aug-Sept), so parts demand can be staged by week and county. (Insider claims; verify in 30 crew-chief interviews.)
ideas.first_90_days: Interview 30 crew chiefs and 10 large-farm owners on downtime cost and parts waits; sign 8 crews to paid winter inspections; hire 6 ex-dealer techs; buy PRO Service access and one multi-brand tool; line up a reinsurer or fronting carrier for the 24-hour credit; build the first parts-cache list from crews' own failure logs; price test $12k/$16k/$20k per machine-season.

ideas.title: Shared Shop
ideas.one_liner: Run the shop for clusters of large farms: embedded lead techs, a shared regional bench and parts cache, maintenance planned around the farm's field calendar, priced per machine per year with an uptime promise and shared savings.
ideas.customer: Row-crop and specialty farms of about 6,500+ acres or $5M+ in sales (my estimate 20-25k such farms; the 2022 Census counted 105,384 farms at $1M+, producing over 75% of sales), each with 30-120 machines and a shop with 1-3 techs.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Owner/COO or CFO. Budget: the repairs line plus shop payroll and parts stock, consolidated into one per-machine fee; sold on cost per acre and the cost of a lost planting or harvest day.
ideas.problem: Big farms keep shops because dealers are slow and expensive (a Titan executive says most shop rates now exceed $140/hour), but one to three in-house techs cannot cover five brands, electronics, hydraulics and aftertreatment, skip services at peak, quit for dealer pay, and each farm hoards its own parts stock. Nobody sells the outsourced alternative.
ideas.solution: Take over the shop. The farm's own techs transfer in (bigger bench, training and career path improve retention); a regional bench covers electronics and hydraulics; 6-12 neighboring farms share a parts cache; maintenance plans follow the field-operation calendar and machine data; pricing is a fixed per-machine fee plus pass-through at cost plus a share of savings against the trailing three-year repair spend.
ideas.why_now: Dealer-parity tools lower the barrier to running electronics-heavy fleets without a dealer; dealer technician shortage (NAEDA: average dealer would hire five more) slows service; trough-year cost pressure (Deere cut prices on ~190k parts in 12 months and expects 15-20% lower 2026 sales); US tractor unit sales fell from 288,187 in 2020 to 195,857 in 2025 (secondary source), so fleets are older.
ideas.wedge: One county cluster in Iowa/Nebraska/Kansas: three farms of 8-15k acres and one hub shop at the center. Run a 30-day baseline of three years of repair spend and downtime, then propose shared savings. First ten customers: farms where the dealer relationship is already strained.
ideas.path_to_100m: 500 accounts x about $200k all-in annual repair, maintenance and shop labor (my estimate: a 6,500-acre farm at $25-30/acre in machinery repair and maintenance plus technician payroll) = $100M of gross billings, about 2% of the estimated 20-25k farms above $5M. Gross margin 15-20% (my estimate), so large revenue and modest profit at first; the value is the bench, the data and the density.
ideas.who_does_it_today: In-house farm shops; dealer fleet and contract-hire service packages (I found a UK precedent at a 10,000-acre farm and no US equivalent); Deere Operations Center tools and JD Protect for new machines; independent mobile mechanics; farm-management companies that do not employ techs.
ideas.why_they_lose: Dealers bill hours at roughly 60% service margin and cannot sell a fixed fee that rewards fewer breakdowns, nor service other brands; OEM tools are single-brand; independents lack capital and a bench.
ideas.moat: Switching costs (our people, tools, records and parts cache live inside the customer's operation) plus scale economies in shared bench and parts across clusters.
ideas.earned_secret: A large-farm shop manager knows the real cost is the five-day planting or spray window: a down planter can cost more than a year of shop payroll. He also knows his two techs skip routine services at peak, and that every farm in the county hoards parts because dealer lead times are unpredictable, so inventory that could be shared sits idle. (Insider claims; verify.)
ideas.first_90_days: Interview 20 shop managers; sign 3 pilot farms in one cluster; collect three years of repair invoices and downtime logs; hire a lead tech and a parts coordinator; draft the shared-savings contract with a farm-law attorney; lease the hub shop.

ideas.title: Machine Passport
ideas.one_liner: The PSA/ACV of farm machinery (collectibles authentication-plus-liquidity pattern): a serial-keyed condition grade and service-and-telemetry history for used tractors, combines and sprayers, sold to lenders, auctions, dealers and buyers, with warranty and financing attached at the sale. It has not happened because the record-holders are single-brand counterparties and only dealer tools could read full machine history until the settlement.
ideas.customer: Ag lenders (Farm Credit associations, community banks, independent leasing companies), auction houses, dealer used-equipment managers, and used-machine buyers.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Lender head of equipment finance or collateral management (appraisal and portfolio-monitoring lines); auction VP operations (condition-report line); dealer used manager (trade-in appraisal). Buyers pay for inspections at the sale.
ideas.problem: There is no TractorFax. A buyer of a $300k used combine relies on an hour meter, the seller's word and a goodwill call to a dealer. OEM certified pre-owned covers only late-model, low-hour units of one brand (Deere: 8R/9R tractors up to 3 model years and 1,500 hours; S-Series combines up to 2 years and 1,000 hours). Dealers hold the real service records but are counterparties, so they never publish them. Lenders mark collateral blind.
ideas.solution: Publish an inspection standard and grade; sell inspections through auctions and lenders; build a serial-keyed record from independent shops, auction reports and machine-data reads (using the dealer-equivalent tools independents now have the right to use); sell lenders monitoring and residual marks; attach warranty and financing at the sale; later add a dealer-to-dealer wholesale exchange for aged inventory.
ideas.why_now: Settlement parity gives independents access to what only dealers could read; the downturn leaves lenders marking collateral blind; Tractor Zoom's Q2 2026 dealer playbook reports chronic aged inventory in 4WD tractors over 425 hp and a trough into late 2026-2027; dealer machinery inventories were $5.72B in Dec 2025 (farmdoc).
ideas.wedge: Inspection and report for the largest used units (combines, 4WD and high-horsepower tractors, sprayers) sold through two auction houses and ten lenders in one region; publish the standard openly.
ideas.path_to_100m: All my estimates (I found no sourced used-transaction count and do not use the unverified $70-100B 'used market' figures): 25,000 inspections x $1,100 = $27.5M; 150,000 history/valuation lookups x $60 = $9M; 400,000 equipment loans/leases monitored x $75/year = $30M; warranty and financing attach on 15,000 sales x about $1,200 = $18M; wholesale fees $10-15M. About $95-100M. That needs roughly a quarter of high-value used transactions and a third of equipment lenders: heroic, a 6-8 year outcome.
ideas.who_does_it_today: OEM certified pre-owned (Deere, Case IH/New Holland, AGCO); Machinery Scope (independent inspections, appraisals and warranty since 2013); Tractor Zoom (dealer market data); TractorHouse/Machinery Pete listings; auction condition reports (Purple Wave, BigIron, RB Global). I found no multi-brand serial-keyed history product.
ideas.why_they_lose: OEMs and dealers are the counterparty and cover only their own brand; auctions earn on volume and carry no condition risk; lenders have no data.
ideas.moat: Network economies (every shop, auction and lender adds records, raising the value of each serial's history) plus switching costs (lender covenants and monitoring reference the grade) and counter-positioning against OEM and dealer.
ideas.earned_secret: The hour meter is the least informative number. Idle-time ratio, derate events, controller replacements, reflashes and operating conditions predict remaining life, and only dealer tools could read them until the settlement. (Inference; I did not verify which fields the tools expose.)
ideas.first_90_days: Define the grade sheet with three master techs and two lenders; run 100 paid inspections at two auctions; test which data fields PRO Service and a multi-brand tool actually expose; sign one lender for a 500-loan pilot.

ideas.title: Tech Bench
ideas.one_liner: Travel-nurse-style bench (capex pass-through to a scarce trade): OEM-neutral farm-equipment technicians on 13-week W-2 contracts who follow the planting and harvest waves from state to state, with a short-program training pipeline financed by employers and the new Workforce Pell. It has not happened because ag is small to national staffing firms and technician credentials are brand-specific and dealer-tied.
ideas.customer: Farm-equipment dealers, independent shops and large-farm shops that cannot fill technician jobs.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Dealer GM or service director (contracted-labor and recruiting lines), billed hourly (my estimate $85-95) against shop rates they resell at over $140.
ideas.problem: Technicians constrain every other idea here. BLS counted 36,830 farm equipment mechanics in May 2023 (mean pay $52,120). NAEDA says the average dealer would hire five more; 70% of dealers planned technician hires in 2025; in a Sept 2023 poll 65% of dealers expected revenue losses above 9% from vacancies and 34.7% above 20%. Demand is a wave, not a level.
ideas.solution: Employ technicians (benefits, housing stipend, tool truck, OEM-neutral certification), rotate them south to north with the seasons, place them 13 weeks at a time, and build the feeder with 8-15 week programs paid by employers, using Workforce Pell where a program qualifies.
ideas.why_now: Workforce Pell began July 1, 2026: programs of 150-599 clock hours, awards roughly $1,260-$4,310 for 8-15 weeks, 70% completion and 70% placement tests, governor and Education Department approval, and programs must have run a year first. The settlement shifts demand toward independents that have no recruiting machine; trough-year dealers avoid permanent hires but need peak coverage.
ideas.wedge: Spring-planting 2027 bench of 25 techs for 15 dealers and shops in the Upper Midwest, recruited from underused dealer techs and diesel programs.
