ideas.path_to_100m: About 650 full-time-equivalent techs x 1,700 billed hours x about $90 = $99M, roughly 1.8% of the 36,830 BLS-counted farm equipment mechanics. Gross margin 22-28% (my estimate). Pell is a subsidy, not the revenue (1,000 trainees at about $3k Pell plus about $6k employer fees is roughly $9M).
ideas.who_does_it_today: Dealer recruiting and OEM programs (Deere recruits at the Farm Progress Show; Caterpillar reportedly wants its dealers to hire 40,000 techs in two years); staffing firms (e.g., Aventure Staffing places diesel techs at a Minnesota ag dealer at $24-33/hour); AED Foundation; community colleges and trade schools. I found no ag-specific travelling bench.
ideas.why_they_lose: Dealers compete for the same techs and are franchise-bound; generalist staffing firms offer no neutral credential, housing or tool trucks; schools cannot deploy.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (a loyal, credentialed bench) plus scheduling process power across regional waves. This is the weakest moat in the set: it is the labor spine for the other ideas and a staffing business until the credential has value.
ideas.earned_secret: Brand certification does not travel with the tech, yet most of any repair (hydraulics, electrical, engine) is brand-agnostic; a neutral credential plus a bench that follows the wave fills peaks without anyone hiring permanently. (Inference; verify with 15 service directors.)
ideas.first_90_days: Interview 20 service directors on peak-season gaps and what they would pay; recruit 10 pilot techs; set up employer-of-record and workers' comp; contract one community college for an 8-week pilot; check Workforce Pell eligibility in two states.

ideas.title: Any-Shop Plan
ideas.one_liner: Mechanical-breakdown coverage and an uptime promise for out-of-OEM-warranty tractors, combines and sprayers that pays any qualified shop on a preferred price schedule, underwritten from machine data and sold through lenders and used-equipment sales.
ideas.customer: Operators of late-model, high-value machines outside OEM warranty.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Farm operator or CFO (repair reserve). Distribution signers: lender equipment-finance head, auction VP, dealer used manager.
ideas.problem: Lumpy repair bills in a downturn. OEM plans are dealer-locked: Deere PowerGard requires dealer service (a $500 deductible per work order on large tractors); RDO Ready+ is dealer-backed; HSB's farm equipment breakdown cover excludes tractors and combines. Machinery Scope (CNA-backed, up to 10-year-old machines, tractors/combines/sprayers) is the one real independent.
ideas.solution: Underwrite from fault history and condition grade (Machine Passport); price by system (engine and aftertreatment, drivetrain, hydraulics, electronics); pay certified shops on a negotiated labor and parts schedule; supply exchange components (Core Bank); add a loaner for harvest and planting (Pit Crew). Sell at lender funding, auction sale and annual renewal.
ideas.why_now: Parity tools make fault data readable outside dealers; farm-income pressure and a 2026 trough; independent repair is now legitimate.
ideas.wedge: Used combines, sprayers and 4WD tractors 3-10 years old sold through two auctions and four lenders in the Plains, with one admitted or fronting carrier.
ideas.path_to_100m: As carrier or program manager booking premium: 20,000 contracts x $5k = $100M, about 4-5% of an estimated 450k late-model high-value machines outside OEM coverage (my estimate; no sourced count). As a pure MGA keeping about 25%, it needs about 80,000 contracts (about 18%): heroic. Legal premise: commercial service contracts can be treated as insurance where no exemption exists (NCOIL), so build through a licensed insurer or reimbursement policy, which adds time and capital.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Machinery Scope (CNA-backed); Deere PowerGard and JD Protect; New Holland Service Plus and other OEM plans; AGCO programs; dealer programs (RDO Ready+); HSB equipment breakdown for implements and electronics.
ideas.why_they_lose: Their plans exist to route dealer labor and genuine parts; paying an independent at about $90/hour instead of $140+ would cannibalize the 61.5%-margin service line and OEM parts margin, and they cannot price risk from data they do not share across brands.
ideas.moat: Process power (loss-ratio edge from data, shop schedule and reman) plus counter-positioning against dealer-routed plans.
ideas.earned_secret: Dollar losses cluster in a few systems (engine and aftertreatment, drivetrain, hydraulics, electronics) and are usually foreshadowed by fault-code frequency and fluid condition that the OEM can see and an independent underwriter can now read; the largest controllable cost is price per claim (shop rate and part price), not claim count. (Insider claim; verify with claim files.)
ideas.first_90_days: Find a fronting carrier and reinsurer; collect 12 months of repair invoices from 20 shops for loss costing; build a rate sheet by system; pilot with one lender on 200 funded machines; get a state-by-state legal opinion on the product form.

ideas.title: Standard Shop
ideas.one_liner: NAPA AutoCare for farm equipment: certified multi-brand independent shops under one brand, a 12-month or 2,000-hour repair guarantee honored by any member, one parts and credit program, and farmer-facing booking.
ideas.customer: Independent ag and diesel shops (1-8 techs) that already do most installs.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Shop owner (dues plus purchases through the program); farmers pay through the repair invoice.
ideas.problem: Farmers who would save an estimated 20-40% still use the dealer because nobody stands behind an independent repair and the dealer has the tools, parts and credit. Deere's Harvest Terms (0% until after harvest on its Multi-Use Account; $4.87B of revolving charge receivables at FY2025) is a retention weapon no independent can match. NAEDA (a dealer trade group) says nearly 60% of dealer-sold parts are installed by someone else and the average dealer supplies nine independent shops.
ideas.solution: Certification standard (tool access, training, insurance), a nationwide guarantee backed by a reinsurer, a parts program (OEM via dealer, second tier, aftermarket, reman), a credit program, lead generation and booking.
ideas.why_now: Settlement parity; the AFBF memoranda (Deere, CNH, AGCO, Kubota and others, reported as 70-80% of equipment sold) give independents manuals and tools beyond Deere; trough-year cost pressure.
ideas.wedge: 40 shops across IA/IL/NE/KS under a published standard; guarantee launched with a reinsurer; one parts hub.
ideas.path_to_100m: 500 member shops x about $200k a year through the program (parts, reman, supplies) = $100M, plus dues of about $600/month ($3.6M). This is parts-distribution economics (22-28% gross margin, my estimate). I found no census of independent shops; my estimate is 8-12k shops touch farm equipment, so 500 is about 5%.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Dealer parts counters; Summit Tractors' partner network (single brand); mail-order and salvage suppliers. I found no multi-brand ag network or franchise.
ideas.why_they_lose: Dealers are single-brand franchisees and cannot endorse rivals' repair; OEMs cannot guarantee non-OEM work without conceding the service margin.
ideas.moat: Brand (the guarantee) and network economies, plus purchasing scale. Brand takes years to build.
ideas.earned_secret: Independents do not lose jobs on price; they lose on trust and parts credit. A shop owner knows farmers will switch for 25% off if the shop can promise any network shop will fix it free if it fails, and no single shop can promise that. (Verify.)
ideas.first_90_days: Interview 30 independent owners; sign 15 founding shops; draft the standard and warranty with a reinsurer; test a parts program through two dealers' wholesale accounts and one aftermarket distributor.

ideas.title: Core Bank
ideas.one_liner: Win the cores and own independent remanufacturing of farm machine components: pay cash for failed engines, hydraulic pumps and motors, final drives, transmissions and electronic modules, remanufacture to OE spec with a warranty, and sell back on exchange.
ideas.customer: Independent shops, farm shops and custom crews; dealers as overflow.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Shop owner or farm shop manager; parts cost of goods sold.
ideas.problem: OEM reman (Deere's: through dealers, up to about 30% cheaper than new, up to a 2-year warranty on transmissions and axles) runs on cores that dealers return to the OEM stream. Independents scrap or lose cores, and until now could not flash a replacement controller. An industry source says agricultural engine cores are hard to find in the US even though demand is high.
ideas.solution: A national cash-for-core program through shops and farm shops; a central plant with testing and flashing capability; a brand-agnostic catalog (engines from Cummins, FPT, Perkins, Yanmar and Kubota are shared across brands); next-day freight; a warranty backed by a reinsurer.
ideas.why_now: Settlement parity plus PRO Service reprogramming makes used and reman controllers installable by independents; Deere expects about $1.2B of 2026 tariff expense (about 3x 2025), raising new-part costs; new tractor unit sales fell from 288,187 in 2020 to 195,857 in 2025 and combines from 5,030 to 3,579 (secondary source), so repairs on older machines rise; CNH and Tractor Zoom see 2026 as the trough.
ideas.wedge: Hydraulic pumps and motors, hydrostatic drives and final drives for the top five combine and tractor platforms; one plant in Iowa or Nebraska; core buying at 150 shop locations. First ten customers: the ten largest independent shops plus three custom crews.
ideas.path_to_100m: About 35,000 exchanges a year at about $2,900 blended (my estimates: 4,000 engines at $9k, 1,000 transmissions at $12k, 6,000 hydraulic pumps and motors at $3.5k, 4,000 final drives and axles at $5k, 14,000 turbos, injectors and small items at $800, 6,000 electronic modules at $1,500) = about $105M. I have no sourced count of component failures; at a 3-5% annual event rate across roughly a million higher-value machines the reman-able event pool is far above 35,000, so this is under 10% of events (verify in shop job logs). Anchor: Deere Reman employs over 500 people at five Springfield-area sites plus a core center of over 200.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Deere Reman; AGCO Reman; engine makers' programs; local rebuilders and independent sellers (reman Kubota engines listed with $2,000-2,500 core charges); All States Ag Parts/Parts ASAP (used, aftermarket and reman, 24 locations); Deere's new second-tier parts.
ideas.why_they_lose: OEM reman runs through dealers who return cores to the OEM and cannot buy cores from independents or rebuild rival brands; local rebuilders cannot flash controllers or offer a national warranty.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (the core stream) plus scale economies in testing and flashing, and process power in OE-spec reman.
ideas.earned_secret: In reman the product is the core, not the rebuilt unit, and Deere treats its core center as the lifeblood of the business. The independent channel is the leak in the OEM core stream, and most failed major components are rebuildable if the housing is sound. (Insider claim; verify.)
ideas.first_90_days: Interview 20 shops on cores scrapped and failure frequency; buy 200 cores of the top five SKUs; contract a rebuild partner; prove the flashing workflow; price against Deere Reman and OEM new.

ideas.title: Elevator Depots
ideas.one_liner: Consigned depots of fast-moving farm parts inside co-ops and ag retailers, delivered by the retailer's own trucks and billed to the farmer's existing retailer account, which settles when grain is delivered; first-party supply includes Deere's new second-tier parts, which Deere says will be sold through 'other places' besides dealers.
ideas.customer: Ag retail and co-op locations (CHS about 400-450, sources conflict; Nutrien over 1,800 retail locations across all markets; Bushel's network covers more than 3,500 grain and ag retail facilities and over 50% of US grain origination) and their farmer customers.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Farmer pays on the retailer account; the co-op or retailer GM/COO signs a consignment program (no capital; commission about 10-12%, my estimate).
ideas.problem: Downtime is parts latency: the dealer counter is 40 miles away and out of stock, and mail order takes days. Dealers cannot add counters without territory and cost conflicts.
ideas.solution: 300-500 SKUs of wear and maintenance parts (filters, belts, chains, bearings, hoses and fittings, knives and sections, sensors, fluids), serial-number fit lookup, auto-replenishment from regional hubs, same-day delivery on the retailer's trucks, and Deere's second-tier alternative parts as first-party supply.
ideas.why_now: Deere says its alternative parts will be sold through dealers and other places customers buy today, and it cut prices on about 190,000 parts; more repairs move to farmers and independents; retailers need non-input revenue in a down farm economy (Nutrien retail sales $17.6B in 2025, slightly down); Bushel launched a Lien Protection Program in July 2026 to digitize grain settlements.
ideas.wedge: 40 co-op sites in two states, one hub, 300 SKUs chosen from independent shops' job logs.
ideas.path_to_100m: 600 depots x about $170k consigned sales = about $102M (my estimate: a rural parts counter does $300k-$1M, so this is incremental), about 3% of an estimated $3-4B of brand-agnostic wear and maintenance parts. Revenue is gross sales; contribution about 10-15% after the retailer's commission (my estimate).
ideas.who_does_it_today: Dealer parts counters; Messick's, TISCO/SMA, A&I Products, All States Ag Parts (24 locations), Sparex (owned by AGCO since 2010), mail-order suppliers with 35,000+ SKUs, Tractor Supply and farm stores. A cautionary case: La Coop federee in Quebec is exiting machinery parts distribution. I found no US co-op parts-distribution program at CHS or Nutrien.
ideas.why_they_lose: Dealers face territory and cost limits; mail order cannot deliver in hours; farm stores lack serial-fit data and replenishment.
ideas.moat: Scale economies (hub and replenishment density) plus switching costs (account and point-of-sale integration). Moderate to weak.
ideas.earned_secret: A co-op manager's agronomy and fuel trucks visit every farm weekly and his account system already carries the farmer's balance to harvest; what is missing is inventory in the right place. (Common practice; settlement-at-delivery mechanics unverified here.)
ideas.first_90_days: Interview 15 co-op managers; mine 500 repair invoices for the SKU list; negotiate a consignment term sheet with two co-ops; line up Deere second-tier supply and two aftermarket suppliers.

ideas.title: Swap, Don't Buy: AMI-driven redeployment of the installed transformer base
ideas.one_liner: Use smart-meter data to find oversized, lightly loaded transformers and move them to sites where load has outgrown the unit, so a utility buys fewer new ones during a 2-year-plus wait; paid a share of the purchases avoided.
ideas.customer: Co-op and municipal utilities with AMI first (no return on equity to protect), then investor-owned utilities under affordability pressure.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Capital budget line for distribution transformers and system improvements. Co-op/muni: general manager plus engineering manager. IOU: VP Distribution Engineering or Director of Distribution Planning; CFO signs the success fee.
ideas.problem: Public power cannot get units: 80% hold less stock than in 2018, 30% report high risk of running out within a month, and 1 in 5 projects were deferred or cancelled (APPA 2024 brief). Planners size generously and rarely revisit, so many units sit lightly loaded while EVs, heat pumps and storage overload others (DOE's efficiency test assumes about 50% load for liquid-filled units; recalled from memory, verify). Engineers do not trust a swap list because 5-20% of meter-to-transformer records are wrong (Siemens estimate).
ideas.solution: Repair connectivity from AMI voltage and outage correlation plus GIS and a field check; compute each transformer's load shape, hot-spot aging and 5-year growth; generate a swap plan pairing surplus oversized units with overloaded or failing sites; run the redeploy yard (ratio, DGA and PCB test, tag, truck, install); feed what is left into the pooled purchase forecast. Pricing: data subscription plus 25-35% of avoided new-unit cost and avoided failure cost.
ideas.why_now: Lead times over 2 years; PPI for distribution and large power transformers up about 40% real 2020-24 (BLS via CRS); AMI at about 72% of US meters (EIA 2022, 119M); EV, heat-pump and data-center load growth; regulators pushing utilities to exhaust non-purchase options.
ideas.wedge: Single-phase pole-mount and small pad-mount units at 10 AMI-equipped co-ops/munis, reached through state associations and joint action agencies (OMPA, FMPA type). Fee only on swaps that actually happen.
ideas.path_to_100m: Assume 70% of the 1.5M units bought a year (DOE 2021; NREL 1.4-2.4M added/replaced) are at AMI utilities (about 1.05M). Redeployment displaces 10% (105k units) at an assumed $5k average for the swappable class: about $525M a year avoided. A 30% success fee is about $158M if every AMI utility took part; add subscriptions (about 150 IOUs at $300k plus about 1,200 AMI co-ops/munis at $40k, about $90M). $100M needs roughly 35-50% of AMI-enabled utilities: HEROIC. Only plausible if the corrected transformer-to-customer ledger becomes the system of record for EV hosting, DER interconnection, outage and procurement forecasting.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Itron (transformer load management), Landis+Gyr, Siemens EnergyIP equipment load management and meter-to-transformer connectivity analytics, Oracle Utilities (DataRaker; PECO case in T&D World), consultants (Quanta Technology, Burns & McDonnell), and utilities' own planners (free). None found taking performance risk or running physical redeployment (searched; 'none found', not 'none exist').
ideas.why_they_lose: AMI vendors sell per-meter software licenses and avoid truck-roll liability. IOUs earn a return on rate base, so avoiding capex lowers earnings (structural), which is why the first customers are co-ops, munis and performance-based-regulation states.
ideas.moat: 7 Powers: Counter-positioning (against rate-base utilities and licence-selling AMI vendors) plus Process power in the redeploy yard, backed by a cumulative failure and aging dataset.
ideas.earned_secret: The shortage is partly a records problem. 'Half the fleet is over 33 years old' is nameplate age, but real loading is low and the cheapest transformer is already on a pole. Nobody swaps because they do not trust which customers hang on which unit; fix the ledger and the supply appears.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign 3 AMI co-op/muni pilots (free analysis). Deliver a corrected loading map and swap list for one district. Execute 50-100 swaps and measure units avoided and hours saved. Fix the success-fee schedule. Hire an ex-utility planner and a data engineer.

ideas.title: Cores for Coils: a closed-loop second-life factory for retired distribution transformers
ideas.one_liner: Buy utilities' retired and failed transformers on scrap-plus terms, test and strip them, put new coils on good grain-oriented cores, and sell warrantied rebuilt units in 6-10 weeks at about 60-70% of new price.
ideas.customer: Co-ops, munis, industrial plants, solar/storage and data-center developers, and utilities restocking their own yards.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Utility materials/stock budget (capex or inventory): materials manager or VP Supply Chain at an IOU; GM or operations manager at a co-op/muni; procurement or facilities director in industry.
ideas.problem: Lead times over 2 years. About 95% of cores are GOES and about 95% of domestic core steel comes from one mill (CRS), yet a retired unit's core is sold as scrap. Failures are mostly insulation and coil damage; many cores and tanks survive. About half the 60-80M installed units are over 33 years old, so retirements are plentiful.
ideas.solution: Multi-year retired-unit supply contracts with utilities (scrap price plus a share of resale); PCB screening and core-loss testing; a semi-automated coil-winding line that re-coils good cores to the buyer's spec; 1-3 year warranty backed by an insurer; later a large-power-transformer repair and rewind line (the only domestic non-import capacity that scales in about a year).
ideas.why_now: GOES is single-sourced; 50% tariffs on steel and on cores and laminations (CRS); EO 14420 covers 69 kV and up and excludes local distribution; the lane does not depend on virgin GOES. Legal premise to verify: NRECA comments say DOE counsel stated existing and recycled transformers are not covered products, so rebuilt units sit outside the efficiency rule (could not retrieve DOE's 'Rewound and Rebuilt Equipment' section; the June 2026 RFI could change it).
ideas.wedge: One regional plant (about 20k units a year) beside a PCB-licensed processor, fed by 5 co-ops' retired yards. Products: 25-100 kVA single-phase and 75-500 kVA pad-mount. First 10 customers: co-ops/munis in the same state association plus solar developers.
ideas.path_to_100m: Retirements are perhaps 0.8-1.2M units a year (inferred from NREL's 1.4-2.4M added or replaced). Rebuilt units at roughly $2-4k (60-70% of an assumed $3-6k new price for the class) times 40-60k units a year is about $110-240M: 3-5% of annual unit demand and 4-6% of the retirement stream. Not heroic. Large-power-transformer rewinds are a second line: 30 jobs at $1-3M is $30-90M.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Sunbelt Solomon (17 locations; remanufactured equipment and rentals up to 50 MVA), OEM service arms (Hitachi Energy, Siemens Energy, GE Vernova/Prolec), utility in-house rebuild shops, regional rewind shops, used-equipment dealers, and scrap dealers (today's buyers of retired units). A Datacentres.com piece claims used units trade at 78-82% of new (weak source). Sunbelt Solomon is the one to beat; it is rental and big-unit focused.
ideas.why_they_lose: OEMs sell new units and face retooling for 2029. Distributors have OEM exclusives. Small shops lack capital for automation, insured warranties and utility scrap contracts. Utility in-house shops are shrinking through retirement.
ideas.moat: 7 Powers: Cornered resource (exclusive scrap-stream contracts that secure the scarcest input, GOES cores) plus Scale economies in test and winding automation.
ideas.earned_secret: In a core-limited shortage the scrap yard is America's largest hidden supply of GOES. The failure is in the coil, not the iron, and winding labor (not iron) is the constraint you can automate.
ideas.first_90_days: Legal memo on DOE, state and TSCA/PCB rules for rebuilt units and on utility spec acceptance. LOIs for scrap streams from 3-5 utilities. Test 200 pulled units to measure core-reuse yield. Pre-sell 500 units to 3 co-ops with warranties. Line up the warranty insurer.

ideas.title: Gavi for Transformers: a take-or-pay buyers' consortium that underwrites standard-spec capacity
ideas.one_liner: Pool the demand of non-investor-owned utilities and mid-size developers into one binding 3-year take-or-pay on about a dozen standard designs, credit-enhanced by a lender, so manufacturers can finance US capacity and small buyers finally get production slots.
ideas.customer: Co-ops, munis and small IOUs outside RESCO-type programs, plus solar/storage developers needing medium-voltage pad-mounts.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Member utility capex/materials budgets; signers are the GM/CEO and board (co-op boards, city councils), usually through a G&T or joint action agency.
ideas.problem: NRECA says long-term agreements 'don't solve everything, particularly for smaller utilities that don't have the scale'; hyperscalers sign direct supply deals and fund capacity; APPA reports 1 in 5 projects deferred. Pooling works where it exists (RESCO with ERMCO at 10-14 week lead times, United Utility Supply) but only regionally.
ideas.solution: A standard spec book of about 12 SKUs; binding rolling 36-month member forecasts aggregated; take-or-pay frameworks with 2-4 manufacturers including new capacity (Cleveland-Cliffs Weirton, ERMCO Arizona 2027, Hitachi Virginia 2028); credit enhancement from CFC or CoBank or a DPA Title III / DOE commitment; consigned stock at distributors; financing of deposits. Revenue is principal margin (6-9%) or a manufacturer-paid fee, plus financing spread. Pattern transferred: vaccine advance market commitments plus the hospital-GPO / co-op supplier model.
ideas.why_now: Shortage; DPA determinations (Apr 20, 2026) authorise purchase commitments and financial support; new plants need committed volume; the 2029 efficiency-rule review. Why not yet: about 3,000 fragmented, regulated buyers under varying bidding laws, no credit-enhancing counterparty, distributors cannot commit OEM capacity, and OEMs selling direct to small buyers would face channel conflict with distributors.
ideas.wedge: One G&T or joint action agency with 30+ members, 6 SKUs, 100% pre-commit.
ideas.path_to_100m: Assume non-IOUs buy 25-30% of utility units and utilities are about 65% of the $12.4B distribution market (CRS), so about $2-2.6B reachable including small power transformers. $100M of gross revenue is about 4% of that; 25% share is about $650M of sales. The revenue test passes easily but the profit pool is thin: 6-9% gross margin is $6-9M at $100M of sales and about $50M at 25% share. It becomes a real business only with the financing spread, a manufacturer fee for demand certainty, and cross-sell of other T&D materials.
ideas.who_does_it_today: RESCO (272 co-ops and public power districts, ERMCO partnership, about $60M inventory), ERMCO and Arkansas Electric Cooperatives' contract vehicle, United Utility Supply (about 10,000 units), Texas Electric Cooperatives' buying program, OMPA and FMPA joint programs, distributors (Wesco, Graybar, Border States, Irby, KBS, Alamo Transformer Supply), APPA's voluntary transformer exchange.
ideas.why_they_lose: Regional silos; distributors are not capacity underwriters; joint action agencies are state-level; nobody provides credit support that turns forecasts into plant financing.
ideas.moat: 7 Powers: Switching costs (binding forecast plus a standard spec) and Scale economies, with allocation rights as a cornered resource.
ideas.earned_secret: OEMs allocate on forecast certainty, not price. A binding 3-year forecast on a standard SKU, bundled across 200 utilities, is worth more than a 5% discount, and hospital GPOs never took capacity risk.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign 5 anchor members; run a pooled RFQ on 6 SKUs; get 2 manufacturer term sheets with capacity reservations; line up credit support from CFC/CoBank or a surety; counsel on state bidding law, co-op purchasing exemptions and buyer-group antitrust.

ideas.title: TSMC for Transformer Cores: a neutral, automated core-and-coil foundry
ideas.one_liner: Build a US plant that cuts and winds cores and builds core-coil assemblies for dozens of independent transformer makers, new entrants and rebuilders, buying GOES from every mill, because the only domestic mill is now also a competitor.
ideas.customer: Independent distribution and power-transformer makers (DOE counts 34 OEMs), fabless entrants such as Ayr, and repair shops (including idea 2).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Cost-of-goods line for purchased cores and assemblies; VP Operations or Chief Procurement Officer at the OEM; CEO at a new entrant.
ideas.problem: About 95% of cores are GOES; about 95% of domestic core steel comes from one mill; half to three-quarters of the cores in domestically assembled transformers are imported, almost all from Mexico and Canada (CRS). Cores and laminations carry a 50% Section 232 duty since Aug 2025. Cleveland-Cliffs petitioned in 2020 claiming cores cut in Canada and Mexico evaded GOES tariffs, and is now building its own $150M transformer plant in Weirton, WV.
ideas.solution: Step-lap cutting, wound-core machines, annealing and robotic stacking; coil-winding cells; standard core families that fabless OEMs and the idea 3 consortium design to; toll or foundry terms with capacity reservations; multi-mill GOES contracts (Korea, Japan, India, Cleveland-Cliffs). Pattern transferred: neo-prime / Hadrian-style automated sub-tier factory and the foundry model.
ideas.why_now: Tariffs; steel-supplier conflict; new OEM plants coming (Hitachi, Siemens, ERMCO, Hyundai) that will want cores; fabless entrants depend on Indian contract factories while the EO and tariffs push toward allied or domestic origin; 2029 retooling. Why not yet: GOES is single-source and core machines take a year or more to arrive, so nobody builds a neutral line without committed volume.
ideas.wedge: Distribution cores for 10 independent OEMs and 5 rebuilders, with committed volumes from ideas 2 and 3. Commitments must precede the machine order.
ideas.path_to_100m: Assumptions: cores (steel plus processing) are 10-15% of transformer price, so about $1.2-1.9B of North American distribution cores and about $0.9B for power transformers. If 40% is non-captive, the independent pool is $0.8-1.1B. $100M is about 9-12% of independent core spend (4-5% of all), roughly 30-40 kt of GOES a year at an assumed $3-3.5k per tonne of finished core.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Captive core lines at OEMs (Prolec GE, Hitachi, ERMCO and others), Mexican and Canadian core makers, lamination houses (Cogent Power, Tempel Steel, Magnetic Metals; named from memory, not verified in searches), Cleveland-Cliffs (steel plus its new plant), Metglas (only US amorphous producer). No startup foundry found.
ideas.why_they_lose: OEMs keep core capacity captive and proprietary. A GOES monopolist moving downstream cannot be a credible neutral supplier. Cross-border core lines carry circumvention and tariff risk.
ideas.moat: 7 Powers: Process power (automation) plus Cornered resource (multi-mill supply contracts), with design-in switching costs.
ideas.earned_secret: Output is gated at the first station: the core. Machines take a year or more to arrive, GOES is rationed, and a miscut core is scrap worth tens of thousands. The plant manager who has begged for steel knows nobody will build a neutral line while GOES is single-source.
ideas.first_90_days: 15 OEM and 5 rebuilder interviews for volume LOIs by core family; mill quotes (POSCO, JFE, Nippon, Cogent, Cliffs); confirm 232 treatment of cores and whether a foreign-trade zone helps; site near rail and cheap power; cutting-line vendor quotes; raise.

ideas.title: Time-to-Power Fleet: build-to-stock multi-ratio substation transformers for whoever signs the interconnection first
ideas.one_liner: Hold a financed fleet of pre-built, multi-ratio 30-100 MVA substation transformers (US or allied origin) and sell, lease or option them for 8-16 week delivery, because utilities cannot order speculatively and developers cannot carry the order.
ideas.customer: Data-center developers and neoclouds, storage and solar developers, and utilities needing a unit at energy-service-agreement signing.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Developer VP Power or CFO (pre-development and collateral budgets); utility chief engineer or VP Supply Chain (rate-base capex once a customer agreement is signed); IPP CTO.
ideas.problem: Utilities need a signed customer before an order is prudent; developers will not commit until power is certain; lead times are 3-4 years. The workaround is speculative private orders ('ordering transformers before we've signed the interconnection agreement', per a colo procurement director in a Datacentres.com piece) and heavy collateral: Dominion $1.5M per MW for customers failing credit tests, AEP Ohio collateral at 50% of minimum charges, Consumers Energy standby letters of credit only. Neoclouds are shut out. Wood Mackenzie says only about 12% of 1,066 GW of requested load is firm.
ideas.solution: A fleet of standardized multi-ratio units pre-approved on several utilities' specifications, supplied by OEMs, the idea 4 foundry and the idea 3 consortium. Lease at 12-15% of unit cost a year, lease-to-own, or sell to the utility at signing; reservation fees; redeploy units from dropped projects. Portfolio effect: single projects are junk options, a pool is near-certain to redeploy. Funded by infrastructure debt.
ideas.why_now: Shortage; new collateral regimes; phantom load; the EO pushes buyers to allied origin. Incumbent limits: regulated utilities cannot speculate, developers cannot commit, OEMs have cyclical-capex scars and build to order.
ideas.wedge: Two voltage classes covering most data-center and storage interconnections (exact classes to be confirmed with utility engineers) and 3 standard MVA sizes; 10 mid-size developers.
ideas.path_to_100m: Revenue is easy; capital and risk are the hard part. 35 units sold a year at an assumed $3M is about $105M. Lease-only: about 280 units ($0.85B of assets at an assumed $3M each) at 12% is $100M. Demand check: Wood Mackenzie projects US data-center capacity rising from 24 GW to 110 GW by 2030, about 14 GW a year; at an assumed 2 units per 100 MW that is about 280 units a year for data centers alone. Fleet turnover of 100-140 units a year would be about 15-25% of annual unit flow if lease-only (HEROIC); selling is far lighter.
ideas.who_does_it_today: FluxCo (procurement, leasing, service, warranty; $26M seed), Ayr Energy (modular build-to-order, Indian factories, 40-72 weeks claimed, $500M+ order book), Sunbelt Solomon (largest rental stock; 20 MVA mobile substation case for a data center awaiting a utility feed), Grid Assurance (spares for transmission owners), OEM stock programs, hyperscalers' direct contracts.
ideas.why_they_lose: Ayr and FluxCo sell to buyers with defined projects; neither carries stranded-project risk on a standard fleet. Sunbelt Solomon rents temporary units. Utilities cannot speculate. OEMs will not.
ideas.moat: 7 Powers: Scale economies in cost of capital and portfolio redeployment (a data asset on queue attrition), plus switching costs from utility specification approvals.
ideas.earned_secret: Queue attrition is the hidden asset. Most requested load never gets built, so a single order is a bad option, but about 80% of substation transformers are the same few designs with different nameplates, so a standard fleet redeploys.
ideas.first_90_days: Get 3 utilities' engineers to sign off on one multi-ratio design; secure slot options from 2 allied-origin OEMs; get an infrastructure-credit term sheet; collect refundable reservation LOIs from 3 developers; counsel on hoarding optics and EO exposure.

ideas.title: Time-to-Restore Cover: parametric outage insurance plus spares access for owners nobody covers
ideas.one_liner: Sell independent power producers, data centers and industrial plants a contract that pays per day, and delivers a pre-qualified spare and crew, if a named main transformer is down more than N days, filling the gap between 12-24 month insurance indemnity periods and 3-4 year replacement times.
ideas.customer: Non-utility owners of main step-up and substation transformers (solar, wind, storage and gas owners, data-center operators, industrial sites) and their lenders and tax-equity partners.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Owner's CFO or VP Risk and Insurance; lenders' reserve covenants (some now require developers to fund future replacement). Brokers (Marsh, Aon, WTW) as channel.
ideas.problem: FM identifies transformers as a primary business-interruption driver with replacement times exceeding common indemnity periods (Insurance Business AU). In the Waratah Super Battery transformer failure the owner reportedly could not force a faster replacement. Insurers cannot hold inventory or force delivery; OEMs will not promise dates; Grid Assurance and EEI STEP serve transmission-owning utilities on cost-based rates and do not cover merchant or data-center owners.
ideas.solution: A fleet inventory by spec cluster (MVA, voltages, impedance, bushings) with condition scores; reserved access rights to spares held by several pools (rental fleets, OEM stock, idea 5); pre-negotiated transport and install crews; a parametric payout triggered by SCADA-verified outage after day N; reinsurance capacity; MGA fee.
ideas.why_now: Lead times of 3-4 years; documented BI gap; lender demands after EO 14420; data-center build-out from 24 to 110 GW by 2030 expands the uncovered base.
ideas.wedge: GSUs at two IPP or yieldco portfolios plus 5 colocation operators.
ideas.path_to_100m: Assume about 12,000 non-utility main transformers averaging $2M, so $24B of replacement value (assumption; EIA plant counts not pulled). A 1.0-1.5% annual price is $240-360M. $100M is 28-40% of that pool: HEROIC, and the weakest idea on size, unless data-center build-out roughly triples the insured base.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Grid Assurance, EEI STEP, NATF RESTORE, APPA transformer exchange, FM Global, Zurich and HSB (equipment breakdown plus BI), Sunbelt Solomon (rentals), OEM service contracts, FluxCo (leasing, service, warranty).
ideas.why_they_lose: Each owns one piece (cash payout, spare unit, crew) and none will sign a time-bound restoration obligation; utility-owned pools cannot extend cost-based rate-base pooling to merchant owners.
ideas.moat: 7 Powers: Scale economies (pooling cost per owner falls with size) plus data on common-mode failures by vintage and maker.
ideas.earned_secret: A spare shared by 20 owners costs one-twentieth, but only within a spec cluster. Failures are not independent (a bushing batch, one maker), so pooling must be by spec and vintage, and insurers price physical damage but leave the multi-year lead-time tail uninsured.
ideas.first_90_days: Collect 3 IPP fleet inventories; build a first-pass actuarial model from public failure statistics; talk to 3 reinsurance MGAs and 2 spare-pool operators; get lender letters of interest.

ideas.title: Achilles for the Grid: the supplier-paid, accredited trust network under Executive Order 14420
ideas.one_liner: Run the accredited qualification network (ownership and sub-tier bill-of-materials tracing, firmware attestation, witness inspection and a warranty/spares wrap) that DOE's pre-qualified-vendor list and lenders' replacement-reserve demands will need, paid by suppliers to be listed and by buyers per purchase.
ideas.customer: Equipment suppliers (transformer, breaker, inverter and battery makers), asset owners and developers, lenders and tax-equity investors.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Suppliers: head of US sales or compliance. Buyers: Chief Procurement Officer, CISO or VP Supply Chain at utilities, IPPs and data-center operators, plus general counsel. Lenders via covenants.
ideas.problem: EO 14420 (Aug 26, 2026; one source says 14421) bars acquisition, import, transfer or installation of foreign-produced bulk-power equipment (69 kV and up) tied to 24 countries once DOE determines risk; DOE rules are due Dec 24, 2026; DOE may create pre-qualified vendor lists and licensing and may order installed equipment isolated, monitored or removed; lenders already require developers to fund replacement. Data centers had used Chinese units to shorten lead times (Wood Mackenzie). Each utility audits new foreign factories alone, and questionnaire platforms do not reach factory floors.
ideas.solution: A sub-tier risk taxonomy (bushings, tap-changer controllers, monitoring modules, relays, firmware); supplier subscriptions; per-purchase attestation; witness testing; continuous monitoring; a surety partner for replacement cost; seek DOE recognition as assessor or accreditor. Modeled on UK utilities' UVDB (supplier-paid, buyer-shared) and the CMMC third-party-assessor model.
ideas.why_now: EO 14420 with a 120-day DOE clock; roughly three-quarters of one utility's bids now come from foreign suppliers; installed-base exposure. Filter check: named enforcer (DOE) but rules unwritten; the 2020 predecessor order was suspended and never reinstated; the buyer loses the ability to buy or install if enforced. Treat Dec 24, 2026 as a 10-week option.
ideas.wedge: An 'exposure audit' of installed foreign-origin gear for data-center and IPP owners, leading into purchase attestations.
ideas.path_to_100m: Assumptions: 15,000 covered purchases a year (transformers, breakers, relays, inverters, batteries) at $20k is $300M; plus about 1,500 suppliers at $15k is $22M. If DOE orders inspection of installed units, a weak source says over 8,000 Chinese high-power transformers were imported 2022 to Oct 2025; at $50-150k each that is $0.4-1.2B once. $100M is 25-30% of the recurring pool or 10-25% of the installed-base pool: HEROIC and enforcement-dependent.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Fortress Information Security (A2V network, over 40,000 vendors and 300,000 assets managed; AEP joint venture; Goldman Sachs stake), Interos, Exiger, Everstream, Resilinc, OT security vendors (Dragos, Claroty, Nozomi), test and inspection majors (UL Solutions, DNV, TUV, Intertek, Bureau Veritas), customs brokers, and DOE itself (free list).
ideas.why_they_lose: Questionnaire platforms do not touch factories or hardware; inspection majors are slow, global and certify the same factories; the government lacks staff to run a list.
ideas.moat: 7 Powers: Cornered resource (regulatory recognition) plus Network economies (list once, share results) and data.
ideas.earned_secret: Provenance is decided at the sub-tier. The unit is Korean but the bushings, tap-changer controller or monitoring module may not be. Someone who has walked factory floors and read BOMs knows which 12 components carry the risk and how to check them.
ideas.first_90_days: Read the EO and DOE's request for information; build the component taxonomy; sign 3 owners for exposure audits; recruit ex-DOE, NERC or utility supply-chain people; partner with an accredited inspector; file comments before Dec 24.

ideas.title: Virtual Transformers: buy capacity from the installed fleet instead of the factory
ideas.one_liner: Contract to deliver extra megavolt-amperes at existing substations in months (cooling upgrades, bushing, tap-changer and current-transformer swaps, dynamic ratings, load transfers), priced per MVA unlocked at a fraction of new-unit cost, for utilities and data centers that cannot get a new transformer for 3-4 years.
ideas.customer: Transmission and substation planning at utilities; large-load customers funding upgrades (customer-funded, utility-owned); IPPs.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Utility T&D capital budget (capex deferral): VP Transmission Planning or Chief Engineer. Data-center developer VP Power (preconstruction / energization budget).
ideas.problem: Large substation units are past 3 years, generator step-up past 160 weeks (Q1 2026) and high-voltage breakers at 125 weeks (AJOT/Reuters). Nobody sells 'MVA delivered in 9 months'; planners work to nameplate and OEMs sell new units.
ideas.solution: Thermal modeling to IEEE C57.91 plus DGA and age; hardware kits (fans, pumps, radiators, ester fluid, limiting bushings, tap changers, CTs); sensors and dynamic-rating software; switching and load-transfer studies; a $/MVA-year price with a performance guarantee backed by an insurer.
ideas.why_now: Multi-year lead times; Wood Mackenzie projects data centers could reach 40% of electrical equipment demand (from under 2% in 2020); data centers pay for speed; EO 14420 narrows import options for 69 kV and up.
ideas.wedge: Substations with N-1 headroom at 5 transmission owners; data-center campuses sitting on existing substations.
ideas.path_to_100m: Assumption: the US buys about $5B of power transformers a year at about $50k per MVA, roughly 100 GVA. Unlocking 8-10% is 8-10 GVA at an assumed $10-12k per MVA: $80-120M. Needs roughly 10% of annual capacity additions to come from uprating: heroic-ish.
ideas.who_does_it_today: OEM service arms (Hitachi Energy, Siemens Energy, GE Vernova/Prolec) selling uprating and life extension; Doble and Weidmann; monitoring vendors (Hitachi TXpert, Siemens Sensformer, Qualitrol, GE Kelman); consultants (Quanta Technology, Black & Veatch, Burns & McDonnell); utilities' own planners.
ideas.why_they_lose: OEMs sell new units, so uprating cannibalizes them; planners follow nameplate standards and rate-base incentives; consultants bill hours, not megawatts; nobody guarantees MVA.
ideas.moat: 7 Powers: Counter-positioning against OEM service arms and rate-base planners, plus a fleet-level condition and rating database.
ideas.earned_secret: Nameplate is a contract, not physics. Capacity is often limited by bushings, tap changers, CTs and planning rules, not by copper.
ideas.first_90_days: Pick 3 substations; run rating studies; propose a pilot with a performance guarantee; hire an ex-OEM thermal engineer; sound out one state commission on cost treatment.

ideas.title: The Tele-Inspection Factory
ideas.one_liner: A licensed, insured private provider whose inspectors sign off from a desk on guided video that tradespeople capture on their own phones, priced per inspection, starting with Florida single-trade finals.
ideas.customer: HVAC, water heater, roofing, electrical and solar-plus-storage contractors that pull 300+ permits a year in private-provider states; later building departments and outsourcers that need overflow inspection capacity.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Contractor owner or operations manager, paid from the permit-coordinator and inspection-wait labor line. In a city, the building official signs an on-call contract paid from the fee-funded enterprise fund.
ideas.problem: A building inspector's day is mostly driving and waiting windows, so inspection stays labor-bound even after plan review is automated. Supply is shrinking (an older ICC survey found 30% of code officials planned to leave within five years) and NYC DOB application-to-approval time rose from 8.3 days in 2020 to 20.3 days in 2025 per the NY State Comptroller (July 2026).
ideas.solution: The contractor follows a trade-specific guided checklist (water heater: T&P discharge, venting, strapping, gas connection); the app pre-screens completeness; a licensed inspector reviews the clips (target 25-40 inspections a day) and issues the pass/fail card; failures escalate to an in-person local partner. Price $45-75 per inspection (my estimate).
ideas.why_now: Florida HB 803 (signed May 6, 2026; effective July 1, 2026): 10-business-day clock, 5 for single-trade, deemed approval on a miss, no local plan-review or inspection fees when a qualifying private provider does the work. Florida s. 553.791(8) (2025 text) says private-provider inspections 'may be performed in person or virtually'. HB 683 (2025) allows automated single-trade plan review and added solar and storage. Utah SB 185 (2024) and Texas HB 14 (2023) allow third-party inspection when the city is late.
ideas.wedge: Florida single-trade residential finals (water heater, HVAC changeout, reroof, panel swap, solar-plus-storage). First 10 customers are contractors pulling 500+ permits a year, with registrations in 5-8 large counties.
ideas.path_to_100m: $100M / $60 = about 1.7M inspections a year. No national inspection count is published; my estimate is 60-100M permit inspections a year (from BLS inspector headcount and ~$10-11B wages), so this is about 2% of the pool. Reachable contractor-paid base: AHRI 2025 shipped ~9.3M water heaters, 3.64M heat pumps and 3.25M gas furnaces; only a minority of replacements are permitted (NRDC: ~10% of residential HVAC replacements in California), so permitted trade finals are maybe 3-5M a year nationally (my estimate) and the private-provider and fallback states might hold ~30% of that, or 1-1.5M finals. The idea therefore needs roughly 10-15% of that base plus a few city overflow contracts.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Municipal remote-video pilots (NYC DOB; West Hartford, which found remote took 2-3x longer per inspection); Inspected.com ($2.2M Series A, contractor-side); Sitewire ($3M seed, lender draws); Inspace ($6M, commercial real estate); Built Technologies (lender inspector network with optional remote review); PermitFlow ($91M raised, has an inspection module); Bureau Veritas/CAP Government and Milrose (435+ pros, Littlejohn-owned since June 2026) do in-person private-provider work.
ideas.why_they_lose: Departments are civil-service, jurisdiction-bound and paid per head. Outsourcers bill hours or fee splits for in-person staff. Software firms (PermitFlow, Built) hold no license or E&O and cannot be the signing party. West Hartford's slowdown came from live interactive video; asynchronous guided capture is a different workflow, which is the bet.
ideas.moat: Process Power (guided capture plus an evidence archive that trains the pre-screen, letting one inspector clear far more than the 10-15 in-person visits a day) and Cornered Resource (a roster of licensed pros with local registrations and E&O), reached after roughly 100k inspections.
ideas.earned_secret: The inspector's signature, not physical presence, is the scarce asset: most single-trade finals are binary checks of 6-10 visible items, and windshield time plus 4-hour windows eat most of the day. This is a practitioner claim that the first pilot must test.
ideas.first_90_days: Hire or contract a Florida building code administrator or PE (s. 553.791(1)(n)); bind E&O ($1M/$2M for projects up to $5M per (18)); register with 5 counties; sign 5 high-volume contractors; run 500 inspections side-by-side with local inspectors and publish agreement rates and building-official audit results.

ideas.title: Inspection-as-a-Service for the Top Homebuilders
ideas.one_liner: One master contract that replaces the builder's patchwork of city inspection windows, third-party QA walks and lender looks with a single independent inspection crew per division, funded by the city inspection fees the builder no longer owes.
ideas.customer: Division VPs of construction at the 15 largest production builders, plus mid-size builders (500-5,000 homes a year), in Florida, Georgia, Tennessee, Utah and (as fallback) Texas.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Division president or regional VP of construction signing a master agreement; budget is permit and inspection fees in cost of sales plus the warranty/QA line.
ideas.problem: The builder's schedule is set by inspection waits and failures, not plan review, and each failure costs days. Builders pay the city and then pay again for QA and verification. They also carry their own defect risk: D.R. Horton has been 'almost exclusively self-insured' for construction defects since June 2021, booked $240.1M of legal contingency expense in FY2025 (98% of legal reserves defect-related) and set aside ~$2,348 per home in warranty costs (Lennar ~$3,602) per Hunterbrook's reading of SEC filings. Inspection data has direct P&L value.
ideas.solution: An embedded independent crew (private provider where statute allows) does code inspections same or next day, captures structured trade-by-trade evidence that feeds the builder's QA and warranty system, and optionally lender draws. Price ~$900-1,500 per home, funded by the statutory fee reduction (s. 553.791(2)(b): the locality must cut the fee by its savings and may not charge inspection fees for private-provider work).
ideas.why_now: Florida HB 683 and HB 803; Georgia's 2019 private-provider framework; Tennessee PC 771; Utah SB 185. Also 45L (the $2,500/$5,000 energy-efficient home credit) ended for homes acquired after June 30, 2026 per the IRS, so HERS rating volume (420,135 homes in 2025) is likely to fall and rater businesses are weak.
ideas.wedge: A mid-size Florida builder for two communities, then a top-10 builder's Florida division, then state by state.
ideas.path_to_100m: $100M / ~$1,250 per home = 80,000 homes a year. NAHB counted 909,280 single-family permits in 2025 (Texas 140,002). Top builders build roughly half of US single-family starts (background knowledge). 80,000 homes is ~9% of national single-family starts, or perhaps 20-25% of starts in states with usable private-provider access (my estimate; FL/GA/TN/UT counts not sourced): 3-4 national builders across 5 states. Heroic if only Florida is reachable.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Florida private providers (Universal Engineering Sciences is on Miami-Dade's roster; Bureau Veritas via CAP Government; Milrose), builders' in-house QA, HERS raters, 2-10 HBW/Frontdoor risk management (no field network found), and PermitFlow for permit paperwork (customers include Lennar and Toll Brothers).
ideas.why_they_lose: Private providers are local, price project-by-project and offer no multi-state SLA or data feed. HERS raters are micro-businesses losing credit-driven demand. PermitFlow does paperwork, not inspections. Cities cannot commit to inspection windows.
ideas.moat: Switching Costs (embedded in the builder's QA and warranty data and scheduling) and Scale Economies in routing density.
ideas.earned_secret: The inspection fee is already in the budget; the real value is cycle time and defect data. Waiting on and failing inspections costs more than review time.
ideas.first_90_days: Pitch a builder VP of construction a two-community pilot; pre-register with the counties; run side-by-side with city inspections and report re-inspection rate, days saved and defects caught before drywall.

ideas.title: Technical Control plus Latent-Defect Warranty for Attached Housing (an NHBC for the U.S.)
ideas.one_liner: Independent staged inspections during construction that unlock an insured 10-year structural warranty, sold to condo and townhome developers who otherwise cannot price or insure defect liability.
ideas.customer: Condo and townhome developers in states that tied liability relief to warranty plus third-party inspection (Colorado now; Washington and Oregon moving); later single-family builders who want to move self-insured defect exposure off balance sheet.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Developer CFO or VP of development, from the construction-defect/wrap liability insurance and soft-cost lines; Colorado's law is designed to lower those premiums.
ideas.problem: Condo construction is choked by defect litigation. The US lacks the UK structure because FHA dropped its 10-year warranty requirement effective March 14, 2019 (the HUD-92544 completion warranty remains) and big builders self-insure and arbitrate, so nobody inspects systematically for an insurer's benefit.
ideas.solution: A registered third-party technical-control firm inspects at foundation, waterproofing/envelope, framing, MEP rough and final to a published standard, issues the certificate that satisfies the statute, and an admitted insurer or MGA writes the 1/2/6-year (later 10-year) cover priced off the inspection data. Revenue is the inspection fee plus a share of premium.
ideas.why_now: Colorado HB 25-1272 (signed May 12, 2025): opt-in warranty (1 year workmanship, 2 years plumbing/electrical, 6 years major structural) plus third-party inspection during construction leading to the certificate of occupancy. Washington HB 1403 passed (signing unconfirmed). Oregon HB 3746 cuts condo repose from 10 to 7 years from 2026. California AB 1903 died Aug 31 per The Close (the Construction Defect Journal still showed it pending; verify). Frontdoor paid $585M for 2-10 Home Buyers Warranty (closed Dec 2024).
ideas.wedge: Front Range Colorado townhome and condo developers, first 5 projects, with a carrier or MGA partner.
ideas.path_to_100m: UK analog: NHBC registered 115,350 homes in 2025 with revenue of about GBP 250M per Wikipedia (unreferenced), roughly GBP 2,170 per home. At ~$2,800 per home, $100M = ~36,000 homes a year, about 4% of US single-family permits or perhaps 12-15% of attached-for-sale units (my estimate of ~250k; unsourced). It needs 8+ states to adopt or builders to buy voluntarily. Heroic and legislation-dependent.
ideas.who_does_it_today: 2-10 HBW (Frontdoor; claims ~1 in 5 new US homes; no systematic inspection network found), construction-defect and wrap insurers, builders' self-insurance (D.R. Horton), local third-party inspectors, and Colorado's own program rollout. No US NHBC exists.
ideas.why_they_lose: Warranty administrators earn premium minus claims and have no field force. Big builders self-insure. Cities cannot carry liability to buyers. Inspection firms have no balance sheet. Each fails at one leg.
ideas.moat: Cornered Resource (a proprietary as-built defect and claims dataset that improves loss ratios, plus regulatory designation as program inspector) and Switching Costs.
ideas.earned_secret: Code compliance is not what kills condos; the liability tail is. The statute makes inspection the price of admission, and the first underwriter to see inspected-building loss data sets the price.
ideas.first_90_days: Read the Colorado program rules and qualify as an inspector; sign 2-3 Front Range developers; negotiate a quota-share with an admitted carrier or MGA; write the five-stage technical standard.

ideas.title: The Platform Behind Independent Private Providers
ideas.one_liner: A licensing, insurance, software and payments platform that lets individually licensed engineers, architects and building code administrators run private-provider practices without running a firm, like an independent broker-dealer for inspectors.
ideas.customer: Supply side: solo and small-firm licensed professionals. Demand side: builders and contractors that choose private providers.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The affiliated professional pays a 20-25% platform fee out of fee revenue; the builder or owner pays the professional. Signer is the licensed professional.
ideas.problem: The statute puts liability on the licensed individual (a building code administrator, engineer or architect, s. 553.791(1)(n)) with $1M/$2M or $2M/$4M professional liability and a 5-year tail (s. 553.791(18), 2025 text). Solo pros cannot scale registrations, notices, scheduling, billing and insurance, and corporate firms cannot hire enough licensed signers.
ideas.solution: A platform with a group E&O program, a jurisdiction registry and notice automation, dispatch, tele-inspection and automated single-trade plan-review tools, instant pay, and a brand that builders and building officials trust. Pros keep ~75-80%.
ideas.why_now: HB 803 limits local re-review of private-provider-approved plans and cuts commercial fees up to 50%, so volume is arriving; the old market was too small to justify a platform.
ideas.wedge: Recruit 50 Florida private providers from published city rosters (for example Miami's) with lower group E&O and overflow work from 5 anchor builders.
ideas.path_to_100m: $100M net at a 22% take = ~$450M of gross professional billings. I could not find Florida's private-provider fee pool; my rough guess is $0.7-1.5B (assumption), which would mean roughly 30-60% of Florida, so multi-state (GA, TN, TX, CA, UT) is required. Heroic; the bottleneck is gross-to-net.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Employed-pro firms (Universal Engineering Sciences, Bureau Veritas/CAP, Milrose, regional engineers). No platform found.
ideas.why_they_lose: Firms must employ and insure the signer; Bureau Veritas and Milrose sell mostly to municipalities; software firms avoid licensure.
ideas.moat: Cornered Resource (E&O program plus local registrations), Scale Economies in insurance buying, and Network Economies between pros and builders.
ideas.earned_secret: Supply is individuals with personal signature liability. The scarce inputs are E&O capacity and registrations, not software; independents earn more alone but cannot handle the admin.
ideas.first_90_days: Get a quota-share E&O program quoted for 50 pros; sign 5 builder anchors; onboard 20 pros in 3 counties.

ideas.title: Fixed-Price Special Inspection and Closeout
ideas.one_liner: Replace time-and-materials special inspection and testing on commercial projects with a fixed price per project, remote review, digital evidence and a guaranteed closeout package the building official accepts.
ideas.customer: General contractors and owners of nonresidential projects (tilt-up warehouses, data halls, schools, hospitals) in IBC jurisdictions.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Owner or GC testing-and-inspection allowance; signer is the GC project executive or owner's rep; the building official approves the agency (IBC Chapter 17).
ideas.problem: IBC Chapter 17 requires owner-engaged special inspection, and a Statement of Special Inspections is often a condition of permit approval. Firms bill hours and trips, and final reports arrive late and hold the certificate of occupancy (insider claim to verify).
ideas.solution: Technicians capture structured evidence (rebar, anchors, welds, fireproofing, concrete) with photos and sensors; a PE reviews remotely; reports auto-assemble in the building official's format; a live dashboard shows closeout status.
ideas.why_now: Inspector shortage and construction-boom schedule pressure; Census data center spending hit $50.7B annualized in April 2026, up 28.1% year on year (AGC).
ideas.wedge: Tilt-up warehouse and data-center-shell GCs in Texas, the Southeast and the Midwest; sign 10 GCs.
ideas.path_to_100m: Pool (my estimate): Census total construction $2.2T minus $882B private residential leaves ~$1.3T nonresidential and public; special inspection and materials testing at 0.5-1% (assumption) is $6.5-13B. Terracon alone reports ~$1.1B in revenue (including geotech and environmental). $100M is 0.8-1.5% of the pool.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Terracon, ECS, Intertek/PSI, Kleinfelder, Braun Intertec and regional labs. I found no VC-backed digital-native firm.
ideas.why_they_lose: Productivity cuts their own billable hours; they are local-office organizations; fixed pricing means taking schedule risk; they do not own software.
ideas.moat: Counter-Positioning plus Process Power, later Switching Costs from embedded closeout data.
ideas.earned_secret: Occupancy dates slip on paper (missing sign-offs and reports), not construction; GCs pay for hours but value the date.
ideas.first_90_days: Get approved as a special inspection agency in 5 target AHJs; run a fixed-fee pilot on 3 warehouse shells; measure closeout days.

ideas.title: Permit-Clean: Verified Permit Status and Closeout at the Closing Table
ideas.one_liner: A rail that tells title agents, lenders and insurers whether a property has open, expired or unpermitted work, and clears it out of the seller's proceeds.
ideas.customer: Title and escrow agents, mortgage lenders and listing agents in Florida first, then Texas, Arizona, California and New York.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Seller at closing via escrow for the cure; the title agency pays for the report. Signer is the agency operations head or lender QC head.
ideas.problem: Title insurance does not insure open or expired permits and a standard title search will not show them; a full municipal lien search does (Florida attorney sources). Lenders will not fund until resolved, sellers learn 10-14 days before closing, and one New York case cost ~$25,000. I found no national incidence statistic.
ideas.solution: (a) A report and API on permit lifecycle and closure across jurisdictions; (b) a closeout service using private providers or engineers (Florida law offers engineer/architect affidavits for concealed work); (c) a title underwriter partnership.
ideas.why_now: Florida private-provider final inspections and the 5-day single-trade clock; title agents are under margin pressure.
ideas.wedge: Tampa Bay and South Florida title agencies, pitched on closings saved.
ideas.path_to_100m: About 4M existing-home sales a year (background knowledge). My assumption: 6-10% have a permit issue in permit-active metros at $1,500-3,000 to clear, a $0.4-1.2B cure pool, plus report fees of $30-60 per order. $100M could be 30,000 closeouts at $2,000 plus 1M reports at $40. All incidence and price inputs are unsourced assumptions.
ideas.who_does_it_today: PermitVista (South Florida; model not verified), PropertyKey IMAPP, municipal lien search vendors, Shovels (permit data; ~$6.5M raised), BuildFax (2015: 30M records, 1,600 jurisdictions), local expediters, and county desks such as Collier County's Building Permit Resolution Services.
ideas.why_they_lose: Title insurers price recorded matters, use standard exceptions and are paid per policy. Cities earn nothing from clearing and are siloed. Aggregators sell issuance, not closure. Expediters are local.
ideas.moat: Network Economies and data (closure outcomes per jurisdiction), Switching Costs in title workflows, and relationships in hundreds of building departments.
ideas.earned_secret: The problem surfaces late. Whoever sees permit status at listing controls the cure and the fee, and many open permits are paperwork gaps that a final inspection can close.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign 10 Tampa/Miami title agents for a pilot report; pre-register a private provider to do finals; measure cases cured and days saved.

ideas.title: The Shot-Clock Concession
ideas.one_liner: Take over plan review and inspection for large departments that now lose volume and fee revenue when they miss statutory clocks, paid a share of retained fees, with the clock guaranteed.
ideas.customer: The top ~250 city and county building departments in states with private-provider or deemed-approval triggers (FL, CA, TX, TN, UT, GA).
ideas.payer_and_signer: City manager or building official, paid from the fee-funded enterprise fund on a revenue share (the Macon-Bibb proposal was a 60-40 split). Signer is the city council or manager after an RFP.
ideas.problem: In Florida a missed 10-business-day clock means deemed approval, and when a private provider does the work the locality cannot charge plan-review or inspection fees (commercial fees cut 50%). Departments lose volume faster than they can hire, and civil-service hiring and procurement cannot deploy the money they have.
ideas.solution: A concession with an embedded team, tele-inspection, partnered AI first-pass checks and queue management with an SLA. The vendor posts a clock guarantee, insured against cure costs if a missed clock causes a deemed approval. Pay is 60-70% of retained fee revenue plus a performance bonus.
ideas.why_now: HB 803 (effective July 1, 2026); California AB 253 (third-party review after 30 days); Austin selected SAFEbuilt in July 2026 for plan review and inspection, showing big cities are outsourcing.
ideas.wedge: Ten mid-size Florida departments ($3-15M of fees) losing private-provider volume: a 90-day overflow contract with a clock guarantee that converts to a concession.
ideas.path_to_100m: At a 60% share, $100M of revenue needs ~$167M of fee revenue under contract: 8 departments at $20M or 40 at $4M. Top-100 department fee revenue is unknown. SAFEbuilt (~1,500 employees, 2,000+ customers) proves the scale exists. It needs a few percent of the ~$10-11B inspector-wage pool but many procurements.
ideas.who_does_it_today: SAFEbuilt (Northeast Inspection Consultants acquisition, Oct 2026), Bureau Veritas/CAP Government, Interwest, Willdan, Milrose, and software vendors (Tyler, Accela, OpenGov, Clariti) with AI plan review from GreenLite ($49.5M Series B), Archistar, CodeComply.AI/CivicPlus and CivCheck/Clariti.
ideas.why_they_lose: Outsourcers staff in person and are paid by hours or fee share, not clock guarantees. Software vendors sell tools priced at a fraction of labor (Denver's ~$4.6M over five years versus a department's payroll) and avoid indemnifying deemed approvals.
ideas.moat: Switching Costs (embedded systems and staff) and Counter-Positioning against hourly consultants.
ideas.earned_secret: The department has the money (fee reserves) but cannot deploy it; sell outcomes, not hours.
ideas.first_90_days: Offer 3-5 Florida departments a 90-day overflow pilot with a guaranteed turnaround; report days saved and fee revenue retained.

ideas.title: Energize-on-Schedule: Inspection, Commissioning and AHJ Desk for Hyperscaler Build Programs
ideas.one_liner: A program-level service that guarantees the inspection, special-inspection, commissioning and certificate-of-occupancy path across a hyperscaler's pipeline, priced against the idle-capital cost it removes.
ideas.customer: About 15 hyperscaler and colocation delivery heads.
ideas.payer_and_signer: VP of construction or head of delivery, from the capex soft-cost line.
ideas.problem: Every site has a different building department, special inspection agency and commissioning vendor. A one-month slip on a ~60 MW site was estimated at over $14M of lost value (secondary blog; ~$0.47M a day by my arithmetic). Census data center construction was $50.7B annualized in April 2026 (+28.1%), and consultancies call zoning and permitting a primary bottleneck.
ideas.solution: A standardized program with pre-registered private provider and special inspection agencies, one commissioning-data pipeline, a scheduling desk and a guaranteed temporary-certificate-of-occupancy date, insurance-backed.
ideas.why_now: Hyperscaler capex above $600B in 2026 by several estimates. Texas Governor Abbott paused TCEQ permits for data centers on Sept 21, 2026, showing how regulatory friction can bind (environmental, not building).
ideas.wedge: Virginia, Texas and Arizona colocation developers; one or two sites, using existing third-party programs such as Loudoun's optional third-party inspection program.
ideas.path_to_100m: Commissioning is 0.75-2% of construction (1.5-3.5%+ for critical facilities) and special inspection plus AHJ liaison add maybe 0.5% (assumption). On ~$60B of construction a year (between the $50.7B April rate and an unverified $75B July pace) the pool is ~$0.75-1.5B, so $100M is 7-13%, or 10 buyers at $10M each. Heroic.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Milrose, Terracon, Intertek, Bureau Veritas, SAFEbuilt in some jurisdictions, owner's reps (JLL, Cushman, Jacobs, AECOM), commissioning specialists, and the hyperscalers' own teams.
ideas.why_they_lose: Local fragmentation; owner's reps bill by the hour; labs bill time and materials; no one can guarantee dates.
ideas.moat: Process Power and Switching Costs, plus a Cornered Resource in AHJ approvals.
ideas.earned_secret: The cost is the date, not the fee. Power and transformer lead times (36 months in one report) may bind first, in which case the product becomes commissioning and integrated-systems-test scheduling.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign one colocation developer's Northern Virginia or Texas site for a commissioning-plus-AHJ pilot; map every sign-off; guarantee one temporary-certificate-of-occupancy date.

ideas.title: Capital Projects Desk: the financeable-package standard for association repairs
ideas.one_liner: Turn a liability-driven engineering report into a vote-ready, lender-ready, bid-leveled package and run the project, so boards stop buying repairs from one bid and a PDF.
ideas.customer: Boards of condo and co-op associations with Phase-2 milestone repairs, roofs, envelope, elevators or paving. First 10: Florida buildings of 100-400 units with a fresh Phase-2 report, referred by 2 engineering firms and 2 mid-size managers.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The association, from the project budget (an owner's-rep/soft-cost line, 3-5% of construction cost; Stone Building Solutions, Souffront and DSS Condo already sell this line in Florida). Signer is the board president or treasurer; a lender or credit platform adds a package fee.
ideas.problem: The Phase-2 report is written to limit the engineer's liability, not to win an owner vote. Volunteer boards get one or two bids, cannot compare scopes, pay 30-50% deposits to contractors with no lien-waiver control, and cannot hand a lender a draw schedule. Engineers cannot procure or guarantee price and contractors cannot be neutral. Capacity is scarce (AKAM Southeast cites a shortage of engineers and restoration contractors; one inspection quote rose from $32k to $50k in six months).
ideas.solution: (1) Re-scope into phased options with three vote-ready budgets; (2) 3-5 leveled bids from pre-qualified contractors priced against a growing cost database; (3) lender-ready package with draw schedule, lien-waiver gating, retainage rule and independent monthly verification; (4) owner's rep through completion. Revenue is a percentage of construction value plus lender package fees; the cost database and contractor performance scores are the scalable assets.
ideas.why_now: Florida structural reserves must be fully funded from Jan 1 2026 with no waiver; the Phase-2 pipeline is at least 1,575 buildings in two years (OPPAGA Jul 2026, undercounted); Fannie's 15% reserve floor starts Jan 4 2027; PE is buying restoration contractors (Fortify Restoration, KLH/CPR), so contractor-side bundling becomes the default unless an independent standard exists.
ideas.wedge: Phase-2 package for Florida buildings at 2.5-3.5% fee for the first 10, in exchange for the right to keep anonymized cost data and a lender referral right.
ideas.path_to_100m: 4% x $2.5B of construction value managed per year = $100M, about 830 projects at a $3M average. Florida structural alone is about $2.4-3B/yr (my arithmetic: 1,575 Phase-2 inspections in 2 years x $3M, undercounted), so it cannot carry this alone; nationally it needs about 8% of the $31.1B a year associations put into reserves (a proxy for capital spend, FCAR 2025) across roofs, paving, elevators and envelope. Heroic for one state; requires multi-state, multi-category.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Owner's-rep firms (Stone Building Solutions, Souffront Engineering, DSS Condo); engineering firms doing construction administration; management-company project departments (Associa, FirstService Residential); PE-backed restoration contractors bundling scope (Fortify Restoration/Osceola Capital, KLH/CPR); lender-side draw software not aimed at associations (Built Technologies, Rabbet, Oracle Textura, Handle, CoFi). No national association-specific cost benchmark found.
ideas.why_they_lose: Owner's reps are local and relationship-based with no shared data; engineers are barred by independence from procuring; contractors cannot be neutral; draw software serves lenders on new construction, not volunteer boards.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource plus process power: a cost and contractor-performance database that compounds with every project; becomes network economies if lenders adopt the package as the accepted format.
ideas.earned_secret: The 12-24 months between a Phase-2 report and a shovel are almost all owner vote, money and bid leveling, not engineering; engineers write scope for liability, and the same building can yield a 'do now' list priced well below the full-scope number (hypothesis; validate on 10 real reports).
ideas.first_90_days: Take 5 Phase-2 reports pre-bid with 2 engineering partners; run 5 competitive bids; build the first 200-line cost table; sign one Florida bank and one title underwriter for draw administration; hire an ex-GC estimator and an ex-bank construction lender. Check Florida engineer/contractor independence and the competitive-bidding rule attributed to HB 913 (single vendor source).

ideas.title: Living reserve study: the annual, lender-accepted reserve record (Fannie's three-year clause)
ideas.one_liner: Sell an annual, signed, machine-readable reserve record as a subscription, because Fannie reportedly only trusts a study less than three years old as a substitute for the 15% test.
ideas.customer: Condo and co-op boards below 15% reserve allocation, managers with 50-300 associations, later lenders and insurers. First 10: 25 Florida and California associations with a loan or sale event in the next 12 months.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Board treasurer, from the reserve-study/professional-fees line ($2.5-20k+ per traditional study every 3-5 years; $5.5-16.5k+ for a Florida SIRS; vendor-blog figures).
ideas.problem: From Jan 4 2027 a project must show 15% of budgeted assessment income going to reserves, or (per secondary sources) a current independent study whose highest recommended allocation is funded. A study older than three years is worthless to a lender, traditional firms deliver one PDF every few years, credentialed capacity is thin, and Florida's Dec 31 2026 SIRS deadline for coordinated buildings lands the same quarter.
ideas.solution: Annual field refresh by local technicians with drone/photo capture and LLM-assisted component quantification, signed each year by a credentialed professional; cost-indexed funding plan; automatic 15% test and cheapest-compliant-budget what-if; API and signed letter for lenders and insurers. About $2-3k per association per year.
ideas.why_now: The three-year clause turns a decade-cycle purchase into an annual one; Limited Review ends Aug 3 2026; the Florida SIRS cycle peaks Dec 2026.
ideas.wedge: Free 15%-test and funding what-if for managers; paid annual refresh for associations with a pending sale or loan.
ideas.path_to_100m: About 40,000 subscribers x $2.5k = $100M, i.e. about 10.7% of all 373k associations (FCAR 2025), or a much larger share of the condo/co-op subset. Heroic; weakest of the eight.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Association Reserves and Reserve Advisors (incumbent study firms, decades of data); engineering firms; SmartProperty (formerly eReserve) launched 'Atlas' in June 2026, described as a living reserve intelligence engine on 20 years of study data, which is near-identical positioning; management software modules. A hidden incumbent is live.
ideas.why_they_lose: Study firms are paid per report and carry E&O per signature; software vendors lack the credential. Honest caveat: SmartProperty may simply sell the living layer to the same study firms, so this survives only if lender acceptance plus owned credentialed signers is the differentiator.
ideas.moat: Switching costs (annual record and history) and a cornered resource (credentialed signers plus a component database); weak.
ideas.earned_secret: Most of a study is desk work (quantities, unit costs, schedules); lenders need independence, currency and machine-readability, not precision. The three-year clause is the tell (hypothesis).
ideas.first_90_days: Get 3 lenders to confirm in writing that an annual signed record satisfies the reserve test; produce 25 studies at half cost to prove margin; hire 2 RS/PE signers. Confirm the three-year substitution is in Fannie's final text (only secondary sources; the Fannie PDF returned 403) and that Florida SIRS needs an engineer/architect visual inspection.

ideas.title: Ledger-underwritten association credit (CondoConta for the US)
ideas.one_liner: A non-bank lender-of-record for association repair loans, underwritten from live management-company ledgers and funded by capital markets, with a partner bank keeping the deposits.
ideas.customer: Boards facing $1M-$20M roof, structural, envelope or elevator projects. First 10: Florida Phase-2 buildings of 100-400 units introduced by 3 managers and 2 engineers, $1.5-6M loans.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The association, from assessments (debt service replaces a special assessment). Board president or treasurer signs after the owner vote where documents or statute require (majority per secondary summaries of HB 913; a law-firm page says 75% is the default for special assessments when documents are silent).
ideas.problem: Associations can borrow almost only from banks, which lend to win the deposit and which the manager, not the board, usually picks. Bank appetite is capped by concentration limits; paper is short, floating or balloon; there is no secondary market. Gaps like Champlain's ($16.2M of repairs against $0.7M cash) are now routine in Florida.
